flesh mart.example: She might have struck downriver for the ports at Meereen and Yunkai and Astapor, but Rakharo warned her that Pono’s khalasar had ridden that way, driving thousands of captives before them to sell in the flesh marts that festered like open sores on the shores of Slaver’s Bay.

pillow house.meaning: A house where men pay women for sex; a brothel.
pillow house.example: “My people hold that there is no shame to be found in the pillow house.

get one's oar in the water.meaning: A rude joke meaning to have sex.
get one's oar in the water.example: “You got your oar in the water quickly.
forms: got your oar in the water

snarks and grumkins.meaning: Imaginary monsters from children's stories, like bogeymen.
snarks and grumkins.example: You give that black brother the men he seeks, rid the city of some hungry mouths, yet make it all seem mockery so none may say that the dwarf fears snarks and grumkins.

presume on.meaning: To take unfair advantage of someone's kindness; to rely on it too boldly.
presume on.example: If you think to presume on his lordship’s kindness, though, you’ll find me waiting after m’lord has gone, y’see.

lay waste.example: And they must be trained as well, or they will lay my kingdom waste.

hollow drums.meaning: People who make big fierce boasts or threats but have nothing inside; all noise and no real strength.
hollow drums.example: Cersei had managed to buy herself three hollow drums; they would make all the fierce booming sounds she required, but there was nothing inside.

murder hole.meaning: A hole in a castle ceiling through which defenders drop rocks or hot oil on attackers below.
murder hole.example: The last time, torches had burned all along the tunnel, and the eyes of starving men had peered down through the murder holes in the ceiling.

heavy bracelet.meaning: A metal ring locked around a prisoner's wrist; handcuffs or shackles.
heavy bracelet.example: A man has a thirst, wearing these heavy bracelets.

strike home.meaning: To hit the intended target; to have the intended effect.
strike home.example: They’d had to shout and scream and throw stones, and it wasn’t until a few of Arya’s stones struck home that the direwolf had finally stopped following them.

egg one on.meaning: To urge someone to do something, often something wrong or risky.
egg one on.example: Lommy egged him on. “Go on, take it off him, I dare you.”

turnpike stairs.meaning: A narrow winding staircase inside a tower.
turnpike stairs.example: Castles are not friendly places for the frail, Cressen was reminded as he descended the turnpike stairs of Sea Dragon Tower.

green boy.example: There is small honor in unhorsing green boys.

drown out.meaning: To be so loud that another sound cannot be heard.
drown out.example: Bran had been in the maester’s turret with Rickon talking of the children of the forest when Summer and Shaggydog had drowned out Luwin with their howls.

gut churning.meaning: So horrible or disgusting that it makes your stomach feel sick.
gut churning.example: Under a snowy white mane of hair, Dagmer Cleftjaw had the most gut-churning scar Theon had ever seen, the legacy of the longaxe that had near killed him as a boy.

customs officer.meaning: An official who collects taxes on goods brought into a port by ship.
customs officer.example: As windy as he was vast, he began by asking Winterfell to confirm the new customs officers he had appointed for White Harbor.

put to the sword.example: The men had been put to the sword, all but a handful that Theon had allowed to flee to bring the word to Torrhen’s Square.

do for.example: Doing for a babe, and her still on the tit, that takes a certain sort.

lash out.meaning: To suddenly attack someone with words or blows.

descend on.meaning: To attack a place suddenly; to arrive in force.
descend on.example: Darry men recaptured their lord’s keep but held it less than a fortnight before Gregor Clegane descended on them and put the whole garrison to the sword, even their lord.

lop off.meaning: To cut off with one blow.
lop off.example: What did you imagine they would do, bend the knee meekly while the Hound lopped off some limbs?

put about.meaning: To spread a story or rumor.
put about.example: Nonetheless, if we put it about that her daughter is baseborn and Stannis a cuckold, well…

go sour.meaning: To turn bad; to start failing.
go sour.example: But if the battle looks to be going sour they’ll break, and they’ll break bad.

in league with.meaning: Working secretly with someone, usually for a bad purpose.
in league with.example: “Open, or we’ll know you for outlaws in league with the king’s enemies.

in fits and starts.meaning: With many stops and starts; not smoothly.
in fits and starts.example: Trumpets sounded, a drum began to boom, the drawbridge descended in fits and starts, and Ser Edmure Tully led his men out from Riverrun with lances raised and banners streaming.

what's dead may never die.meaning: The ironborn saying: what has died cannot die again.
what's dead may never die.example: “What’s dead may never die,” Esgred said.

take one's leave.example: To be sure, her smile was a shade tremulous when her brothers took their leave of her on the deck of the Seaswift, but the girl knew the proper words to say, and she said them with courage and dignity.

as you please.example: a market day, people everywhere, and she walks in bold as you please and tears a baby from his mother’s arms.

paint stripes on a toad, he does not bec.meaning: Pretending or dressing up cannot change what you really are.
paint stripes on a toad, he does not bec.example: “Paint stripes on a toad, he does not become a tiger.

the commons.example: He was silent for a time, and then he said, “How did the commons take the news of Cersei’s incest?

low places.meaning: Brothels, cheap drinking places, and other bad parts of town.
low places.example: “This would doubtless involve the four men your man Bronn searched for so diligently in all the low places of King’s Landing.

turn of the moon.meaning: One month; one full cycle of the moon.
turn of the moon.example: “If the winds have been kind, Ser Alliser should reach King’s Landing by the turn of the moon, but whether this boy Joffrey will pay him any heed, I do not know.

hundred and a half.example: Tyrion had the City Watch now, plus a hundred-and-a-half fierce clansmen and a growing force of sellswords recruited by Bronn.

hedge wizard.meaning: A poor wizard who travels from place to place; not trained at the Citadel.
hedge wizard.example: A hedge wizard had told him there would be a bountiful spirit summer before the cold set in, he claimed.

mole's town.meaning: A village south of the Wall with a well-known brothel.
mole's town.example: The grounds seemed deserted this morning, with so many rangers off at the brothel in Mole’s Town, digging for buried treasure and drinking themselves blind.

tears of lys.meaning: The Tears of Lys, a poison that kills.
tears of lys.example: He noted sweetsleep and nightshade, milk of the poppy, the tears of Lys, powdered greycap, wolfsbane and demon’s dance, basilisk venom, blindeye, widow’s blood…

triple decked.example: Lord Stannis’s Fury, a triple-decked war galley of three hundred oars, looked almost small beside some of the big-bellied carracks and cogs that surrounded her.

pox scarred.example: A young mother with a pox-scarred face offered to freely tell them all she knew if they’d promise not to hurt her daughter.

lizard lions.meaning: Big lizard-like animals that live in the swamps of the Neck.
lizard lions.example: “Frogs and fish and lizard-lions, and all manner of birds.

name day.meaning: A birthday; the day each year that marks the day a person was born (in Westeros it is called the day the child was named).
name day.example: She would be ten on her next name day, and she was the saddest child that Maester Cressen had ever known.

ham sized.meaning: As big as a ham (a large piece of pig meat); very big.
ham sized.example: “THE KING IN THE NORTH!” boomed Greatjon Umber, a ham-sized fist hammering at the air as he shouted.

spit out.meaning: To say something angrily and forcefully, as if spitting it from the mouth.
spit out.example: He spat out the name like poison on his tongue.

the lists.meaning: The fenced ground where knights fight in tournaments.
the lists.example: No more than two score will enter the lists, including squires and freeriders.

draw up.meaning: (Of riders or wagons) to come to a stop; to pull up.
draw up.example: They drew up in front of the inn.

man rock.meaning: Worked stone — stone cut and piled up by men into walls and towers (Bran’s wolf-dream word for man’s stonework).
man rock.example: Behind the trees the walls rose, piles of dead man-rock that loomed all about this speck of living wood.

iron price.meaning: The Ironborn custom of paying for a thing by taking it with force (with iron weapons) instead of with gold.
iron price.example: Paying the iron price, it was called.

forester's cabin.meaning: A small plain wooden house in the woods where a forester lives.
forester's cabin.example: A little farther up the road, they glimpsed a forester’s cabin surrounded by old trees and neatly stacked logs ready for the splitting, and later a ramshackle stilt-house leaning over the river on poles ten feet tall, both deserted.

cock one's head.meaning: To tilt one’s head to one side, showing interest or asking a question.

short of coin.example: And have men posted around the Moonrunner, in case the Redwynes find a second guard short of coin.

seasoned wood.meaning: Wood that has been dried and aged so it is strong and ready to use (for building ships).
seasoned wood.example: “The queen’s men have laid claim to all the seasoned wood.”

beside oneself.meaning: Overwhelmed by a strong feeling; so afraid, angry, or happy that one cannot think calmly.
beside oneself.example: No one could recall how they came there, but I’m sure I do not need to tell you that the High Septon was beside himself with terror.

good faith.meaning: Honest and sincere intention; wanting to be fair.
good faith.example: “His father’s bones he shall have, as a gesture of Joffrey’s good faith.”

skin down.example: She held it as long as she could, but finally she had to squat by a bush and skin down her breeches in front of all of them.

camp follower.meaning: A person who follows an army from camp to camp, selling food, drink, or sex to soldiers.
camp follower.example: A camp follower brought in to serve his pleasure on the eve of battle, says a second.

hear of.meaning: To be willing to accept or agree to something; ‘would hear of nothing less’ means would accept nothing less.
hear of.example: It made Tyrion more than a little uneasy to detach so great a part of their already inadequate fleet, depleted as it was by the loss of all those ships that had sailed with Lord Stannis to Dragonstone and never returned, but Cersei would hear of nothing less.

butcher's bill.meaning: The number of people killed or wounded in a battle; the cost in lives.
butcher's bill.example: Ser Jacelyn Bywater delivered the butcher’s bill as he was supping on a cold capon and brown bread in the gloom of his solar.

wash out.meaning: To cancel out; to make (something bad) go away.
wash out.example: “A good act does not wash out the bad, nor a bad act the good.

drowned in butter.meaning: Covered thickly with melted butter, as if sunk in it.
drowned in butter.example: This evening they had supped on oxtail soup, summer greens tossed with pecans, grapes, red fennel, and crumbled cheese, hot crab pie, spiced squash, and quails drowned in butter.

ten years a wolf.meaning: For ten years living as a Stark (whose sign is the direwolf); raised among the Starks.
ten years a wolf.example: Ten years a wolf, and you land here and think to prince about the islands, but you know nothing and no one.

wattle and daub.meaning: sticks woven together and covered with mud, used to make the walls of simple houses.
wattle and daub.example: Ghost was stretched out asleep beneath the wattle-and-daub wall of the granary, but he woke when Jon appeared, bushy white tail held stiffly upright as he trotted to them.

worm eaten.meaning: damaged by worms; full of small holes.
worm eaten.example: The fourth room was oval rather than square and walled in worm-eaten wood in place of stone.

men at arms.meaning: common soldiers who fight on foot, below knights in rank.
men at arms.example: How many knights, how many bowmen, how many men-at-arms?

pot shops.meaning: cheap eating places in town where you can buy a bowl of hot food.
pot shops.example: They walk the same streets, drink in the same winesinks, spoon down their bowls of brown in the same pot-shops.

none the wiser.meaning: still not knowing about something; not having learned the secret.
none the wiser.example: The kingsroad wound its way past Winterfell on its way to the Wall, and Yoren had promised he’d leave her there with no one any wiser about who she’d been.

wet with love.meaning: sexually excited and ready for sex.

a shade over.meaning: a little more than (a number or amount).
a shade over.example: Shae only stood a shade over five feet, yet still he must look up to her… but in her case he found he did not mind.

seventh hell.meaning: a curse; the worst of the seven hells, a terrible place.
seventh hell.example: The one that leads them is a she-wolf, a bitch from the seventh hell.

mean piss-all.meaning: to be worth nothing at all (a rude way to say it).
mean piss-all.example: What he done back in the city don’t mean piss-all.

pack off.meaning: to send someone away, usually to a far place.
pack off.example: Small wonder his grandfather packed him off to the Citadel.

slip anchor.meaning: to leave a port quickly and secretly (said of a ship).
slip anchor.example: “The master of the King’s Galley White Hart plots to slip anchor three days hence to offer his sword and ship to Lord Stannis.

gold price.meaning: buying something with gold money. The ironborn think this is shameful; brave men take what they want in battle (the ‘iron price’).
gold price.example: Is it the gold price you paid, or the iron?

boiled leather.meaning: leather made hard by boiling, worn as cheap armor.
boiled leather.example: A scarred face and a stubble of dark beard showed under his spiked steel cap, and he wore mail over boiled leather, dirk and shortsword at his belt.

starve out.meaning: to force people to give up by keeping food from them, as in a siege.
starve out.example: The Lannisters had piled brush around the tower’s base and set it afire, but the stone would not burn, and Lorch did not have the patience to starve them out.

treat with.meaning: to talk with an enemy or rival to make peace or a deal.
treat with.example: Robb knew how ill-suited a man like Greatjon Umber would be to treat with a man like Renly Baratheon, and he knew that she knew it as well.

like as not.example: Buried in the Old Bear’s skull, like as not.

with child.meaning: Pregnant; going to have a baby.
with child.example: Beneath, she was naked, and huge with child.

mortal remains.example: He demands to see the mortal remains before he opens his gates, but it seems that Renly’s corpse has unaccountably vanished.

take up the gauntlet.meaning: to accept a challenge to fight.
take up the gauntlet.example: And Lord Caron and the others who like to kick will want to take up Ser Cortnay’s gauntlet and hazard all upon a single combat.

stave off.meaning: to stop something bad from happening for a time; to hold back.
stave off.example: If Robb Stark can stave off the Lannisters, he may reign as King of the Trident hereafter, but House Greyjoy holds the north now.

mummer's show.meaning: a false show; something done only to look real, not because it is right.
mummer's show.example: Yet it rankled, to sit here and make a mummer’s show of justice by punishing the sorry likes of Janos Slynt and Allar Deem, while his sister continued on her savage course.

mind one's hands.meaning: to keep your hands to yourself; not to steal or touch.
mind one's hands.example: The men are to mind their hands and speak to these women as little as need be.

call one's banners.meaning: to order your lords to bring their soldiers for war.
call one's banners.example: So far Doran Martell had done no more than call his banners.

drain one's skin.meaning: To drink all the wine from a wineskin (a bag made of animal skin for carrying wine).
drain one's skin.example: He could have stopped swilling it down anytime he cared to, but no, he drained one skin and told Lancel to fetch another.

salt wife.meaning: Among the ironborn, a woman taken as a wife in a raid. She is not married in the usual way and ranks below a true wife.
salt wife.example: “I would be your salt wife, milord.”

get it in one's head.meaning: To come to believe something, often something foolish or wrong.
get it in one's head.example: “Some loose tongues spread tales of the preparations for Tyrek’s wedding feast, and these wretches got it in their heads they should be feasted too.

all of eight.meaning: Only eight (years old); no more than eight.

rotten ice.meaning: A dangerous, uncertain situation, like walking on ice that may break under you.
rotten ice.example: He was walking on rotten ice now, Tyrion knew.

hank of hair.meaning: A lock or coil of hair.
hank of hair.example: Inside were four coppers and a little hank of blond hair tied up with a red ribbon.

green lands.meaning: What the ironborn call the mainland: the lands of other people, far from the sea.
green lands.example: In the green lands, they believe a woman with child means good fortune for any man who beds her.

finger dance.meaning: An ironborn game in which men throw short axes at each other and catch them.
finger dance.example: Three burly men were doing the finger dance, spinning short-hafted axes at each other.

come to blows.example: They found a little gold, a little silver, a great sack of copper pennies, and a dented goblet set with garnets that two soldiers almost came to blows over.

in kind.meaning: In the same way; answering an act with the same kind of act.
in kind.example: Without siege engines there was no way to storm Casterly Rock, so the Young Wolf was paying the Lannisters back in kind for the devastation they’d inflicted on the riverlands.

have one's head.meaning: To have someone killed by cutting off the head.
have one's head.example: “He’ll lick it off me or I’ll have his head.

mind one's tongue.meaning: To be careful about what you say.

apple of the throat.meaning: The Adam's apple: the hard lump at the front of a man's throat.
apple of the throat.example: Quick as that, the black brother’s sword was pressed to the apple of the officer’s throat.

rein up.meaning: To stop a horse by pulling its reins; to come to a stop.
rein up.example: The next morning, a sleek merchant on a grey mare reined up by Yoren and offered to buy his wagons and everything in them for a quarter of their worth.

flake off.meaning: To come off in small thin pieces.
flake off.example: A corner flaked off between his fingers as he unrolled it.

make one's water.meaning: To urinate (a polite old way of saying it).
make one's water.example: So you keep to yourself and make your water in the woods, alone.

near the salt.meaning: In a place of honor at a feast table, seated near the lord.
near the salt.example: He was always summoned for feasts, seated near the salt, close to Lord Stannis.

hem in.meaning: To surround and shut in; to trap.
hem in.example: Cold iron and splintery wood closed off the only holes through the piled stones that hemmed them in.

lantern jawed.meaning: Having a long square jaw that sticks out.
lantern jawed.example: He clattered up the steps, threw open the door… and came face-to-face with a tall, lantern-jawed man in black breastplate and gold cloak.

quarter the twin towers.meaning: In heraldry, to divide a shield into four parts and place a family emblem (here the Frey twin towers) on one part together with other emblems.
quarter the twin towers.example: Little Walder quartered the twin towers of Frey with the brindled boar of his grandmother’s House and the plowman of his mother’s: Crakehall and Darry, respectively.

screen one's march.meaning: To hide an army's movement by placing guards ahead of and beside it.
screen one's march.example: The Old Bear had deployed outriders to either side of the main column, to screen their march and warn of the approach of any enemies, and even there he took no chances, sending the men out in pairs.

shriek red murder.meaning: To scream loudly in fear, pain, or anger (as if being murdered).
shriek red murder.example: Before Bran could blink, the black wolf was flying over the plank, there was blood in the water, the Walders were shrieking red murder, Rickon sat in the mud laughing, and Hodor came lumbering in shouting "Hodor! Hodor! Hodor!"

brood over.meaning: To hang heavily over something, dark and watchful; to think about something in a sad, gloomy way.
brood over.example: Their droppings speckled the gargoyles that rose twelve feet tall on either side of him, a hellhound and a wyvern, two of the thousand that brooded over the walls of the ancient fortress.

scoop up.meaning: To lift someone or something up quickly with your arms or hands.
scoop up.example: Osha scooped him up in her bony arms.

stand aside.meaning: To step to one side and not get in the way.
stand aside.example: He warned her to stand aside and let him do his duty.

take up.meaning: To start doing something as a regular activity.
take up.example: If we lose the war, she ought to take up mummery, she has a gift for it.

hold back.meaning: To keep something or someone back; to stop them from moving forward.
hold back.example: The Mountain heard her out; the next morning he picked her daughter, to be certain she’d held nothing back.

pepper with.meaning: To have small amounts of something mixed through, like grey hairs in a beard.
pepper with.example: His small beard was well peppered with grey, and he wore a leather glove on his maimed left hand.

out of hand.example: The Mountain and his men had horses, but the captives were all afoot, and those too weak to keep up were killed out of hand, along with anyone foolish enough to flee.

in the bargain.example: Aye, and throws his life away in the bargain, and the lives of every man inside those walls.

wrong side of the blanket.meaning: Born to parents who are not married.
wrong side of the blanket.example: Dagmer was no true uncle, only a sworn man with perhaps a pinch of Greyjoy blood four or five lives back, and that from the wrong side of the blanket.

in the king's name.meaning: With the king’s power; because the king ordered it.
in the king's name.example: “They told Yoren to open the gates, they told him in the king’s name.

take a mind to.example: “Aye,” she said, “and hands strong enough to twist a man’s head off his shoulders, if he takes a mind to.

screw up one's face.meaning: To twist your face, showing disgust, pain, or effort.

common cause.meaning: A shared aim that people work together to reach.
common cause.example: Two of the other survivors had made common cause.

swaddling clothes.meaning: Strips of cloth wrapped around a baby.
swaddling clothes.example: Since his marriage to little Lady Ermesande three days past, the other squires had taken to calling him “Wet Nurse” and asking him what sort of swaddling clothes his bride wore on their wedding night.

bill of sale.meaning: A paper that proves something was bought and sold.
bill of sale.example: “An inventory,” Sam said, “or perhaps a bill of sale.

two score.meaning: Forty. A ‘score’ is an old word for twenty.
two score.example: No more than two score will enter the lists, including squires and freeriders.

pillow play.meaning: Private loving talk and play between lovers in bed.
pillow play.example: It grated on him to hear her call Varys m’lord in that tone; that was what she called him in their pillow play.

rock wife.meaning: Among the ironborn, a man’s true wife, born ironborn like himself.
rock wife.example: A man had his rock wife, his true bride, ironborn like himself, but he had his salt wives too, women captured on raids.

night lands.meaning: The Dothraki land of the dead.
night lands.example: Dany bid them kill the weakest of their dying horses, so the dead man might go mounted into the night lands.

the mountains of the moon.meaning: A wild mountain range east of the Vale.
the mountains of the moon.example: The clansmen Tyrion had brought down from their fastnesses in the Mountains of the Moon were loyal in their own fierce way, but they were proud and quarrelsome as well, prone to answer insults real or imagined with steel.

ivy covered.meaning: Covered with ivy, a plant that climbs on walls.
ivy covered.example: That evening they stopped in a village at an ivy-covered inn.

mother of pearl.meaning: The shiny inside of some sea shells, used to make things beautiful.
mother of pearl.example: She loved the statues, the pictures in leaded glass, the fragrance of burning incense, the septons with their robes and crystals, the magical play of the rainbows over altars inlaid with mother-of-pearl and onyx and lapis lazuli.

barrel vaulted.meaning: (Of a ceiling or roof) curved like the inside of a barrel.
barrel vaulted.example: Instead he followed the light, wending his way down the narrow aisles beneath barrel-vaulted ceilings.

light headed.meaning: Dizzy, as if one might fall; feeling faint.

pick of the dungeons.meaning: The right to choose prisoners from the dungeons (to take them to the Night’s Watch).
pick of the dungeons.example: “Lord Eddard gave me pick o’ the dungeons, and I didn’t find no little lordlings down there.

give it up for a bad job.meaning: To stop trying to do something because it is hopeless.
give it up for a bad job.example: Finally Ser Dontos the Red gave it up for a bad job, sat down in the dirt, and removed his plumed helm.
forms: gave it up for a bad job

all a lather.example: Pyp and Toad, all a lather to be a part of the great ranging, were to remain at Castle Black.

man cliff.meaning: A high wall of worked stone; Bran’s wolf-dream word for tall man-made walls.
man cliff.example: Beyond its sky-tall man-cliffs the true world was calling, and he knew he must answer or die.

old way.meaning: The Old Way: the ancient Ironborn custom of taking what they want by force — raiding instead of working or trading.
old way.example: When we still kept the Old Way, lived by the axe instead of the pick, taking what we would, be it wealth, women, or glory.

castle forged.meaning: (Of steel or weapons) made in a castle’s smithy; well-made and strong.
castle forged.example: She slashed down hard, and Needle’s castle-forged steel bit into the grasping fingers between the knuckles.

sire a son.meaning: (Of a man) to become the father of a son; to father a male child.
sire a son.example: Shae is not the first to grace my bed, and one day I may take a wife and sire a son.

rub thumb and forefinger together.meaning: To make the hand sign for money (asking for payment).
rub thumb and forefinger together.example: The sellsword rubbed thumb and forefinger together.

the likes of.meaning: People like; others of the same kind.
the likes of.example: “Knights and lordlings, they take each other captive and pay ransoms, but they don’t care if the likes of you yield or not.”

take leave of one's senses.meaning: To go mad; to lose one’s good judgment.
take leave of one's senses.example: “Sam, have you taken leave of all your sense?
forms: taken leave of all your sense

black cells.meaning: The dark prison cells beneath the Red Keep in King’s Landing.
black cells.example: “Throw him down in one of the black cells.”

the back of one's hand.meaning: A slap with the back of the hand; a harsh rejection.
the back of one's hand.example: You had to learn that even though the one they called Shitmouth had the foulest tongue she’d ever heard, he’d give you an extra piece of bread if you asked, while jolly old Chiswyck and soft-spoken Raff would just give you the back of their hand.

in one's cups.meaning: Drunk; having drunk a lot of wine or ale.
in one's cups.example: Whenever he was in his cups he would call for a reaving song, something loud and stormy that told of dead heroes and deeds of wild valor.

long of wind.meaning: (Of a speaker) talking for too long; boring because of long, empty talk.
long of wind.example: The High Septon was as fat as a house, and more pompous and long of wind than even Pycelle.

poison the well.meaning: To spoil a thing in advance so that others cannot use or believe it.
poison the well.example: In many places it had come before them, poisoning the well for their own true tale.

shy of.meaning: Not having enough of; lacking; not yet having.
shy of.example: Her brother had taken every able-bodied man for the fords, leaving Ser Desmond Grell to command a garrison made up of the wounded, the old, and the sick, along with a few squires and some untrained peasant boys still shy of manhood.

break lances.meaning: To fight with long spears on horseback, as knights do in tournaments; to joust.
break lances.example: The Walders would break lances with the squires of Lord Manderly’s escort, but Bran would have no part of it.

after a fashion.meaning: somewhat; in a way; to some degree
after a fashion.example: Gentle Ser Willem Darry, who must have loved her after a fashion, had been taken by a wasting sickness.

a bitter taste in one's mouth.example: “Then why do I have this bitter taste in my mouth?”
a bitter taste in one's mouth.meaning: a feeling of disgust or regret

a brush with death.example: sobered by his near brush with death

a man after one's own heart.example: A man after my own heart.”
a man after one's own heart.meaning: someone who thinks and feels the way I do

a red smile.example: got a red smile for his trouble
a red smile.meaning: a cut throat (the wound looks like a smile)

a shadow on the wall.meaning: power is an illusion, yet it can still kill

bottle up.example: At first Jon had nursed the hope that Squire Dalbridge would keep the wildlings bottled up in the pass.

make for.meaning: To head toward; to go to.

go over to.meaning: To leave one side and join the other; to defect.
go over to.example: you will go over to them, as the wildling girl you captured once urged you.

cut to ribbons.meaning: To cut into thin strips; to destroy completely.
cut to ribbons.example: They may demand that you cut your cloak to ribbons,

winkle out.meaning: To force out of a hiding place, like picking meat out of a shell.
winkle out.example: to winkle them out of the cave the wildlings would need to come up two at a time.

feather them.meaning: A battle order: shoot them so full of arrows that they look feathered.

man claws.meaning: Swords and weapons. A wolf’s word for the claws men fight with.
man claws.example: the stuff of man-claws and hardskin.

man pack.meaning: A group of humans. A wolf’s word for men together.
man pack.example: the howls of the man-pack, wails of fear and wild shouts, laughter and screams.

house of whispers.meaning: The dark crypts under Winterfell where the dead Starks lie. A wolf-dream name for the tomb.
house of whispers.example: the house of whispers where all men were blind.

third eye.meaning: The inner eye a warg sees through when his mind is inside his wolf.
third eye.example: He closed his third eye and opened the other two, the old two, the blind two.

have one’s fill of.meaning: To have had enough of something; to be tired of it.
have one’s fill of.example: I’ve had my fill o’ blundering in the black.

lose count of.meaning: To no longer be able to keep track of a number, or of time.
lose count of.example: I’ve lost all count o’ such.

chew on.example: Osha chewed on that a moment.

style oneself.meaning: To call oneself by a title; to claim a name or rank.
style oneself.example: styling himself King Stannis the First,

keep a foot in the other camp.meaning: To secretly support both sides in a fight, so you win whatever happens.
keep a foot in the other camp.example: They also kept a foot in the other camp, however, since Stannis’s queen is a Florent,

sun and stars.meaning: a Dothraki term of love for the most important person in your life; "my sun-and-stars" means my beloved
sun and stars.example: Her brother Viserys, Khal Drogo who was her sun-and-stars, even her unborn son, the gods had claimed them all.

king beyond the wall.meaning: the title of the leader of the wildlings, the free folk who live north of the Wall
king beyond the wall.example: “He was King-beyond-the-Wall a long time back.

cloth of gold.meaning: an expensive fabric woven with threads of gold
cloth of gold.example: He was wearing a cloth-of-gold half cape fastened with a miniature spear.

cloth of silver.meaning: an expensive fabric woven with threads of silver
cloth of silver.example: Today he wore flashing cloth-of-silver, with dagged sleeves so long the ends of them pooled on the floor.

all for joffrey.meaning: a mocking nickname the captives give to a prisoner who keeps declaring loyalty to Joffrey
all for joffrey.example: the other captives began to call him All-for-Joffrey whenever the guards weren’t listening.

paragraphs.context: It is always summer under the sea,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Patchface's songs describe a world under the sea where everything is upside down and reversed. He nearly drowned as a boy, and his songs keep that topsy-turvy world alive.
paragraphs.simple: Patchface shook the little bells on his fool's hat. Then he sang in a slow, dreamy voice: 'Under the sea, it is always summer. The sea-wives put sea-flowers in their hair and make dresses out of shining silver seaweed. I know, I know, oh, oh, oh.'

paragraphs.context: The red woman had won her, heart and soul
paragraphs.mainIdea: Selyse now worships only one god, the Lord of Light, not the Seven. The singular 'God, she said, not gods' is deliberate: the red woman has fully converted her.
paragraphs.simple: Selyse said 'God,' not 'gods.' The red woman, Melisandre, had won her over completely, body and soul. She turned Selyse away from the gods of the Seven Kingdoms, both the old gods and the new, and made her worship the one god they called the Lord of Light.

paragraphs.context: four less fingernails to clean and trim
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos jokes that losing finger joints was a favor, since he now has fewer fingernails to trim. The dark humor shows how fully he accepts Stannis's harsh justice.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Stannis had rewarded Davos with good lands on Cape Wrath, a small castle, and the honor of being a knight. But he had also ordered that Davos lose the top joint of every finger on his left hand, as payment for all his years of smuggling. Davos agreed, but only if Stannis himself held the knife — he would take punishment from no lesser man. Stannis used a butcher's heavy cleaver, so the cuts would be clean and straight. Afterward Davos chose the name Seaworth for his new family, and for his banner a black ship on pale grey, with an onion on its sails. The old smuggler liked to say that Stannis had done him a favor, by giving him four fewer fingernails to clean and cut.

paragraphs.context: all ripply Valyrian steel, and the red was Lord Eddard's blood
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya sees her father's sword Ice and his blood in the comet's red tail. It is her grief imagining things, not a real vision.
paragraphs.simple: That night Arya lay on her thin blanket on the hard ground, staring up at the great red comet. It was beautiful and frightening at the same time. Gendry, whom they called the Bull, named it 'the Red Sword' — he said it looked like a sword blade still glowing red-hot from the forge. When Arya narrowed her eyes just right, she could see the sword too, only it was not a new sword. It was Ice, her father's greatsword, made of wavy Valyrian steel, and the red was Lord Eddard's blood on the blade, from when Ser Ilyn, the King's Justice, cut off his head. Yoren had made her look away when it happened, but to her the comet looked the way Ice must have looked afterward.

paragraphs.context: Those were Joffrey's gifts as well.
paragraphs.mainIdea: "Those were Joffrey's gifts as well" is bitter irony: the "gifts" are bruises from Joffrey's beatings. Sansa must dress up and smile for the boy who hurts her.
paragraphs.simple: 'Thank you, ser.' Knowing that Joffrey would make her attend the tourney held in his honor, Sansa had taken special care with her face and clothes. She wore a pale purple silk gown and a moonstone hairnet that had been a gift from Joffrey. The gown had long sleeves to hide the bruises on her arms. Those were Joffrey's gifts as well. When the Lannisters told him that Robb had been proclaimed King in the North, his rage had been a terrifying thing, and he had sent Ser Boros to beat her.

paragraphs.context: What a man sows on his name day, he reaps throughout the year
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Hound invents a proverb on the spot to back up Sansa's lie and save Dontos's life. He pretends it is old wisdom so the king will believe it.
paragraphs.simple: 'The girl speaks the truth,' the Hound said in his rough, grating voice. 'What a man sows on his name day, he reaps all year long.' His voice was flat and uncaring, as if it did not matter to him at all whether the king believed him or not. Could it be true? Sansa had not known. It was just something she had said in desperation, to keep Dontos from being punished.

paragraphs.context: It wasn't the gods who'd been cruel, it was Joffrey
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa does not trust Tyrion's sympathy: it was Joffrey, not the gods, who was cruel to her. She will not accept comfort from a Lannister.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa could not think of a single word to say to him. How could he be sorry for what she had lost? Was he mocking her? It was not the gods who had been cruel — it was Joffrey.

paragraphs.context: I did. My wits.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion's gift is 'My wits' — his cleverness, which he offers to help Joffrey rule.
paragraphs.simple: 'I did,' Tyrion said. 'My wits.'

paragraphs.context: Lions," she whispered, without thinking. She glanced about nervously,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa whispers 'Lions' to correct Tyrion's metaphor: her real danger is the Lannisters. She slips and speaks her fear aloud without thinking.
paragraphs.simple: 'Lions,' she whispered, without thinking. She looked around nervously, but no one was close enough to hear.

paragraphs.context: They cooked it with mushrooms and apples, and it tasted like triumph
paragraphs.mainIdea: "It tasted like triumph" — Cersei savored murdering Robert. The boar that killed him was made delicious by her victory over him.
paragraphs.simple: 'He did that to himself. All we did was help.' When Lancel saw that Robert was going after the boar, he gave him strongwine — Robert's favorite sour red, but made three times stronger than what he was used to. The great stinking fool loved it. He could have stopped gulping it down any time he wanted, but no — he drained one wineskin and told Lancel to fetch another. The boar did the rest. 'You should have been at the feast, Tyrion. There has never been a boar so delicious. They cooked it with mushrooms and apples, and it tasted like triumph.'

paragraphs.context: I was taken by a sudden urge to meet your young lady
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion decodes Varys's polite words: 'I was taken by a sudden urge to meet your young lady' really means 'I know where your girl is' — a threat and a show of power.
paragraphs.simple: 'I'll take some wine.' Tyrion sat down beside Shae. He understood what was really happening here, even if Chella and the girl did not. Varys was delivering a message. When he said, 'I was taken by a sudden urge to meet your young lady,' what he meant was: 'You tried to hide her, but I knew where she was, and who she was — and here I am.' Tyrion wondered who had betrayed him. The innkeeper, that boy in the stable, a guard at the gate … or one of his own men?

paragraphs.context: So tell me—who lives and who dies?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Varys's riddle: power lies where people believe it lies. The sellsword will obey whichever of the three — king, priest, or rich man — he believes truly holds power.
paragraphs.simple: 'In the streets they call it the Red Messenger,' Varys said. 'They say it comes as a herald before a king, warning of fire and blood to follow.' The eunuch rubbed his powdered hands together. 'May I leave you with a little riddle, Lord Tyrion?' He did not wait for an answer. 'In a room sit three great men: a king, a priest, and a rich man with his gold. Between them stands a sellsword — a small man of low birth and no great mind. Each of the great ones orders him to kill the other two. "Do it," says the king, "for I am your lawful ruler." "Do it," says the priest, "for I command you in the names of the gods." "Do it," says the rich man, "and all this gold shall be yours." So tell me — who lives and who dies?' Bowing deeply, the eunuch hurried out of the common room on soft slippered feet.

paragraphs.context: She probably wouldn't even know me now, Arya thought.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya feels guilty about driving Nymeria away; she wonders if her wolf would even know her now, or would hate her.
paragraphs.simple: A she-wolf. Arya swirled her beer, wondering. Was the Gods Eye near the Trident? She wished she had a map. It had been near the Trident that she had left Nymeria. She had not wanted to, but Jory said they had no choice: if the wolf came back with them, she would be killed for biting Joffrey, even though he had deserved it. They had had to shout and scream and throw stones, and it was not until some of Arya's stones actually hit that the direwolf finally stopped following them. She probably would not even know me now, Arya thought. Or if she did, she would hate me.

paragraphs.context: Robert was the true steel. Stannis is pure iron
paragraphs.mainIdea: Noye's metal metaphor: Robert was true steel; Stannis is iron — hard and strong but brittle, he will break before he bends; Renly is copper — pretty but worthless.
paragraphs.simple: The armorer thought about that for a moment. 'Robert was the true steel. Stannis is pure iron — black and hard and strong, yes, but brittle, the way iron gets. He will break before he bends. And Renly, that one, he is copper: bright and shiny, pretty to look at, but not worth very much at the end of the day.'
hardWords: at the end of the day

paragraphs.context: Any sweeter and I would have gagged
paragraphs.mainIdea: Robb hates offering peace so much that gentler terms would almost make him sick — 'Any sweeter and I would have gagged.' He wants revenge, not peace.
paragraphs.simple: 'Any sweeter and I would have gagged.' Robb's beard had grown in redder than his red-brown hair. He seemed to think it made him look fierce, kingly … older. But bearded or not, he was still a boy of fifteen, and he wanted revenge no less than Rickard Karstark did. It had not been easy to talk him into making even this offer, poor as it was.

paragraphs.context: You should have stopped at Imp.
paragraphs.mainIdea: "Dwarf" is a worse insult than "Imp," and Tyrion is warning Slynt: you should have stopped at Imp. Do not push me further.
paragraphs.simple: 'Dwarf?' His anger flashed. 'You should have stopped at Imp. I am Tyrion of House Lannister, and someday — if you have the brains the gods gave a sea slug — you will drop to your knees in thanks that it was me you had to deal with, and not my lord father. Now then, how many sons do you have?'
hardWords: the sense the gods gave a sea slug

paragraphs.context: We'll need three cups for that
paragraphs.mainIdea: "We'll need three cups for that" is a treasonous joke: so many men claim to be king that one toast needs three cups. Many laughed.
paragraphs.simple: Varys covered his mouth with his hand. 'You are very cruel to say so. One last matter. Lady Tanda gave a small supper last night. I have the menu and the guest list for your inspection. When the wine was poured, Lord Gyles rose to lift a cup to the king, and Ser Balon Swann was heard to remark, "We'll need three cups for that." Many laughed …'

paragraphs.context: It was just, what he did to me
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos thinks of everything Stannis gave him and calls the finger-cutting 'just' — fair. It shows his total loyalty to Stannis.
paragraphs.simple: Everything I am, I owe to him. Stannis had raised him to knighthood. He had given him a place of honor at his table, a warship to sail instead of a smuggler's little boat. Dale and Allard captained warships too, Maric was oar-master on the Fury, Matthos served his father on the Black Betha, and the king had taken Devan as a royal squire. One day Devan would be knighted, and the two little boys as well. Marya was mistress of a small castle on Cape Wrath, with servants who called her 'my lady,' and Davos could hunt red deer in his own woods. All this he had from Stannis Baratheon, for the price of a few finger joints. It was just, what he did to me. I had broken the king's laws all my life. He has earned my loyalty. Davos touched the little pouch hanging from the leather cord around his neck. His finger bones were his luck, and he needed luck now. As do we all. Lord Stannis most of all.

paragraphs.context: King Stannis is my god. He made me and blessed me
paragraphs.mainIdea: 'King Stannis is my god' — Davos worships Stannis himself, not any god. He must weigh every word: the inn is crowded and he is hiding who he is.
paragraphs.simple: Davos sipped his ale to buy himself a moment to think. The inn is crowded, and you are not Salladhor Saan, he reminded himself. Be careful how you answer. 'King Stannis is my god. He made me, and blessed me with his trust.'

paragraphs.context: The Seven have never brought me so much as a sparrow
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stannis's hawk story: the Seven are like Proudwing, the hawk that would not fly for him. Melisandre is the new 'red hawk' he will try — he uses her without truly believing.
paragraphs.simple: 'When I was a boy I found an injured goshawk and nursed her back to health. I named her Proudwing. She would sit on my shoulder and flutter from room to room after me and take food from my hand, but she would not soar. Again and again I took her out hawking, but she never flew higher than the treetops. Robert called her Weakwing. He owned a gyrfalcon named Thunderclap who never missed her strike. One day our great-uncle Ser Harbert told me to try a different bird. He said I was making a fool of myself with Proudwing, and he was right.' Stannis Baratheon turned away from the window, and the ghost-ships that moved upon the southern sea. 'The Seven have never brought me so much as a sparrow. It is time I tried another hawk, Davos. A red hawk.'

paragraphs.context: what is given can be taken away
paragraphs.mainIdea: Balon burns Robb's letter: 'what is given can be taken away.' He will not accept a gifted crown; he will take one himself.
paragraphs.simple: 'What is meant is what is said. The boy will give me a crown. And what is given can be taken away.' Lord Balon tossed the letter onto the brazier, on top of the necklace. The parchment curled, blackened, and caught fire.

paragraphs.context: Where? Theon might have asked, but by then he knew.
paragraphs.mainIdea: 'But by then he knew' — Theon suddenly realizes Balon's plan: he will attack the North, not the Lannisters.
paragraphs.simple: Where? Theon might have asked, but by then he knew.

paragraphs.context: the lie died in her throat as a hand grasped
paragraphs.mainIdea: "It's easy," Arya says about killing — but the lie died in her throat. She realizes killing is not easy at all.
paragraphs.simple: 'It's easy,' Arya said, but the lie died in her throat as a hand grabbed the top of the wall. She saw it in the light of the burning town, so clearly it was as if time had stopped. The fingers were thick and rough, wiry black hairs grew between the knuckles, and there was dirt under the thumbnail. 'Fear cuts deeper than swords,' she remembered, as the top of a pot-shaped helmet rose up behind the hand.

paragraphs.context: you are not proving him a liar, you're only telling the world
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion argues that tearing out a man's tongue does not prove him a liar — it only tells the world you fear what he might say.
paragraphs.simple: 'A folly,' sighed Tyrion. 'When you tear out a man's tongue, you are not proving him a liar. You are only telling the world that you fear what he might say.'

paragraphs.context: The things I do for love," he murmured softly
paragraphs.mainIdea: The 'golden man' in Bran's dream is Jaime Lannister, golden-haired: he pulled Bran up, then threw him from the tower, saying "The things I do for love."
paragraphs.simple: 'Fly or die!' cried the three-eyed crow as it pecked at him. Bran wept and begged, but the crow had no pity. It put out his left eye, then his right, and when he was blind in the dark it pecked at his forehead, driving its terrible sharp beak deep into his skull. He screamed until he was sure his lungs would burst. The pain was like an axe splitting his head apart — but when the crow ripped its beak out, all slimy with bits of bone and brain, Bran could see again. What he saw made him gasp with fear. He was clinging to a tower miles high, his fingers slipping, nails scratching at the stone, his legs dragging him down — stupid, useless, dead legs. 'Help me!' he cried. A golden man appeared in the sky above him and pulled him up. 'The things I do for love,' he murmured softly, as he threw him out, kicking, into the empty air.

paragraphs.context: Pycelle's spotted hand was clutching at his beard the way a
paragraphs.mainIdea: 'One, he thought' — Tyrion is counting. Pycelle is the first of three people he is testing, to find out who reports his plans to Cersei.
paragraphs.simple: 'Ah … to be sure.' Pycelle's spotted hand was clutching at his beard the way a drowning man clutches at a rope. It made Tyrion's heart glad. One, he thought.

paragraphs.context: A hound will die for you, but never lie to you
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Hound explains why he likes dogs better than knights: a hound will die for you but never lie to you. Dogs are loyal and honest; knights lie.
paragraphs.simple: 'I like dogs better than knights. My father's father was kennel-master at the Rock. One autumn, Lord Tytos came between a lioness and her prey. The lioness did not care that she was Lannister's own emblem. The bitch tore into my lord's horse, and would have killed my lord too — but my grandfather came up with the hounds. Three of his dogs died driving her off. My grandfather lost a leg, so Lannister paid him for it with lands and a tower-house, and took his son as a squire. The three dogs on our banner are the three that died, in the yellow of autumn grass. A hound will die for you, but never lie to you. And he will look you straight in the face.' He cupped her chin in his hand, lifting it, his fingers pinching her painfully. 'And that is more than little birds can do, isn't it? I never got my song.'

paragraphs.context: "Carry him, he says," he muttered, chuckling.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lommy begs 'You got to carry me,' and the soldier kills him instead, chuckling 'Carry him, he says.' Brutal irony — no mercy for the wounded.
paragraphs.simple: 'Think so?' The man lifted his spear casually and drove the point through the boy's soft throat. Lommy never even had time to surrender again. He jerked once, and that was all. When the man pulled his spear loose, blood sprayed out in a dark fountain. 'Carry him, he says,' he muttered, chuckling.

paragraphs.context: anger makes her stupid. I much prefer angry and stupid
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion deliberately keeps Cersei waiting: 'anger makes her stupid. I much prefer angry and stupid to composed and cunning.'
paragraphs.simple: 'Good. The longer Cersei waits, the angrier she will become — and anger makes her stupid. I much prefer angry and stupid to calm and cunning.' Tyrion tossed his folded cloak into his litter, and Timett helped him up after it.

paragraphs.context: the lion is still, poised, his tail twitching, while the fawn
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion's metaphor: Tywin is the waiting lion, Robb the frightened fawn. Each waits for the other to move, but whichever way the fawn runs, the lion will catch him.
paragraphs.simple: 'There is sitting and there is sitting,' Tyrion suggested. 'Each one waits for the other to move. But the lion is still, poised, his tail twitching, while the fawn is frozen with fear, his insides turned to jelly. No matter which way he leaps, the lion will have him — and he knows it.'

paragraphs.context: Joseth the master of horse engaged in a different sort of riding
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran walks in on Joseth the master of horse having sex with a woman against the wall — 'a different sort of riding' is the joke: Joseth trains horses, but this riding has nothing to do with horses.
paragraphs.simple: They left by the back door instead of walking through the long hall, and Bran bent his head low as they passed through the lord's door. In the dark hallway outside the Great Hall, they found Joseth the master of horse doing a different kind of riding. He had some woman Bran did not know pushed up against the wall, with her skirts pulled up around her waist. She was laughing until Hodor stopped to watch. Then she screamed. "Leave them alone, Hodor," Bran had to tell him. "Take me to my bedroom."
hardWords: engaged in a different sort of riding

paragraphs.context: He prowled beneath the trees, his brother close behind him
paragraphs.mainIdea: From here to the end of the chapter, Bran is dreaming as his direwolf Summer: 'his brother' is the other wolf, 'the man-pack' means humans, and the fearless 'female and the young male' are Meera and Jojen Reed, come to the godswood at night.
paragraphs.simple: He fell asleep with his head full of knights in shining armor, fighting with swords that shone like star-fire. But when the dream came, he was back in the godswood, the holy wood of the old gods. The smells from the kitchen and the Great Hall were so strong that it was almost as if he had never left the feast. He moved quietly under the trees, his brother close behind him. This night was full of life, full of the howling of the man-pack at their play. The sounds made him restless. He wanted to run, he wanted to hunt, he wanted to —

paragraphs.context: he don’t count but to eleven
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dywen's dirty joke: Craster has ten fingers and one penis, so he can only count to eleven — meaning he is too stupid to notice if Dywen steals one or two of his nineteen wives.
paragraphs.simple: Dywen clicked his teeth together a few more times. "Maybe I do remember. Craster has ten fingers and one cock, so he can't count past eleven. He would never miss one or two of them."
hardWords: he don't count but to eleven

paragraphs.context: Our enemies leave our bodies for the crows and the wolves
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dolorous Edd's bleak joke: there is no real difference between a wildling 'friend' and a wildling enemy. Enemies leave your body for the crows and the wolves; friends bury you in a secret grave. Either way, you are dead.
paragraphs.simple: "Do you know the difference between a wildling who is a friend to the Watch and one who is not?" asked the gloomy squire. "Our enemies leave our dead bodies out for the crows and the wolves. Our friends bury us in secret graves. I wonder how long that bear has been nailed up on that gate, and what Craster had hanging there before we came shouting to his door?" Edd looked at the axe doubtfully, with the rain running down his long face. "Is it dry in there?"

paragraphs.context: He gives the boys to the gods
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gilly tells Jon the horror plainly: Craster gives his newborn sons to 'the cold gods' — the white shadows, the Others. That is why there are no boys or men at Craster's Keep, only Craster and his wives and daughters.
paragraphs.simple: "For the baby, not for me. If it is a girl, that is not so bad — she will grow for a few years and then he will marry her. But Nella says it is going to be a boy, and she has had six babies and knows these things. He gives the boys to the gods. When the white cold comes, he does, and lately it comes more and more often. That is why he started giving them sheep, even though he loves the taste of mutton. Only now the sheep are gone too. Next it will be the dogs, until …" She lowered her eyes and stroked her belly.

paragraphs.context: Would you make me your captain for the night
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha (as 'Esgred') and Theon trade sailing words that are also sex jokes: 'make me your captain for the night,' 'steer me safe into port,' 'no one better with ropes and knots.' Every line works two ways — ships and bedding.
paragraphs.simple: "Would you make me your captain for the night, my lord prince?" She had the most wicked smile he had ever seen on a woman.

paragraphs.context: The Drowned God needed a strong oarsman, I fear
paragraphs.mainIdea: 'The Drowned God needed a strong oarsman' is the ironborn way of saying a man drowned. The next line gives the plain truth: Eldiss drank too much wine and his belly burst. Then comes the ironborn prayer: 'What's dead may never die.'
paragraphs.simple: "The Drowned God needed a strong oarsman, I fear," answered the short, solid man with the white streak in his beard.

paragraphs.context: His face broke into a huge gap-toothed smile and he said
paragraphs.mainIdea: The reveal: the stableman greets her as 'Lady Asha.' The bold 'shipwright's wife' Theon has been flirting with all day is his own sister Asha, who gave a false name ('Esgred') to test what kind of man her brother has become.
paragraphs.simple: The lout paid him no attention. His face broke into a huge smile with missing teeth, and he said, "Lady Asha. You're back."

paragraphs.context: asking him what sort of swaddling clothes his bride wore
paragraphs.mainIdea: The squires mock Tyrek Lannister as 'Wet Nurse' because his bride, little Lady Ermesande, is a baby — asking him what sort of swaddling clothes she wore on their wedding night.
paragraphs.simple: Lannister guards stood silent in their red cloaks and helmets with the lion crest. Ser Jacelyn's gold cloaks faced them across the hall. The steps to the throne were guarded by Bronn and Ser Preston of the Kingsguard. Courtiers filled the gallery while people begging favors gathered near the tall oak-and-bronze doors. Sansa Stark looked especially lovely this morning, though her face was as pale as milk. Lord Gyles stood coughing, while poor cousin Tyrek wore his bridegroom's cloak of soft white fur and velvet. Since his marriage to little Lady Ermesande three days ago, the other squires had taken to calling him "Wet Nurse" and asking him what kind of baby clothes his bride wore on their wedding night.

paragraphs.context: You’re certain that they are dead this time
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion publicly mocks Ser Alliser Thorne's warning that the dead walk, offering him spades: 'If you bury your dead, they won't come walking.' The court laughs — but the reader knows Thorne is telling the truth, which makes the joke grim.
paragraphs.simple: "You're sure that they are dead this time?" Tyrion asked gently. When Bronn choked trying not to laugh, Tyrion knew how he should go on. "Truly, truly dead?"

paragraphs.context: make it all seem mockery so none may say
paragraphs.mainIdea: Varys spells out Tyrion's triple move: he gives Thorne the men he asked for, strips Cersei of her guards, and wraps it all in mockery — so no one can say the Hand of the King believes in monsters.
paragraphs.simple: Grand Maester Pycelle had already hurried away, but Varys and Littlefinger had watched it all, from start to finish. "I grow ever more admiring of you, my lord," said the eunuch. "You please the Stark boy by sending home his father's bones, and you take away your sister's protectors, all in one quick move. You give that black brother the men he is asking for, you get rid of some hungry mouths in the city, and yet you make it all look like a joke, so no one can say that the dwarf is afraid of monsters. Oh, cleverly done."

paragraphs.context: On the day of their union, a wife may ask a token of love
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jorah warns Dany why Xaro really wants to marry her: by Qartheen custom, on the wedding day each partner may ask one gift that cannot be refused — Xaro would ask for a dragon, and 'with one dragon, Xaro Xhoan Daxos would rule this city.'
paragraphs.simple: "He tells the truth, as far as it goes, but there is one thing he failed to mention. The people of Qarth have a strange wedding custom, my queen. On the day of their marriage, a wife may ask her husband for a gift of love. Whatever she wants from his riches, he must give her. And he may ask the same of her. Only one thing may be asked, but whatever is named may not be refused."

paragraphs.context: a winged wolf bound to earth with grey stone chains
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jojen's green dream in plain terms: the 'winged wolf' is Bran — a Stark, a warg, touched by the three-eyed crow; the 'grey stone chains' are his broken legs binding him to earth; the crow pecking at the chains is the three-eyed crow trying to free his mind.
paragraphs.simple: Jojen's eyes were the color of moss, and sometimes when he looked at you, he seemed to be seeing something else. Like now. "I dreamed of a winged wolf tied to the earth with chains of grey stone," he said. "It was a green dream, so I knew it was true. A crow was trying to peck through the chains, but the stone was too hard, and his beak could only chip pieces off them."

paragraphs.context: too honest to live, too noble to shit
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion's rule for surviving Cersei: honest, noble men — 'too honest to live, too noble to shit' — are devoured by her. Lords Stark and Arryn would never play her game, and both are dead. Tyrion will play it.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion thought about the men who had been Hand before him, who had been no match for his sister's tricks. How could they be? Men like that … too honest to live, too noble to shit — Cersei eats such fools for breakfast every morning. The only way to beat my sister is to play her own game, and that was something the Lords Stark and Arryn would never do. No wonder both of them were dead, while Tyrion Lannister had never felt more alive. His short legs might make him look like a funny monster at a harvest dance, but this dance he knew well.

paragraphs.context: A man pays his debts. A man owes three
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaqen explains the debt: Arya saved three lives from the fire, and 'only death may pay for life.' The Red God is owed three deaths. Arya may name any three people, and Jaqen will kill them — no more, no less.
paragraphs.simple: "A man pays his debts. A man owes three."

paragraphs.context: your wedding was a mummer’s farce
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stannis and Renly trade cruel jokes about Renly's marriage: it was a 'mummer's farce,' and 'in your bed she's like to die that way' means Renly will never sleep with his wife — the marriage will never be consummated, and everyone at the table knows why.
paragraphs.simple: "We both know your wedding was a mummer's farce. A year ago you were planning to make the girl one of Robert's whores."

paragraphs.context: Knights are sworn to defend the weak, protect women, and fight for the right
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa's faith breaks: knights are sworn to defend the weak and protect women, yet the Kingsguard beat her while the whole court watched. Only the Hound, the fool Dontos, and the Imp — none of them true knights — tried to help.
paragraphs.simple: Some serving girls took charge of her, saying empty comforting words to stop her shaking. One stripped off what was left of her dress and underclothes, and another washed her and cleaned the sticky fruit juice from her face and her hair. As they scrubbed her with soap and poured warm water over her head, all she could see were the faces from the courtyard. Knights are sworn to defend the weak, protect women, and fight for what is right, but none of them did a thing. Only Ser Dontos had tried to help, and he was no longer a knight, no more than the Imp was, nor the Hound … the Hound hated knights … I hate them too, Sansa thought. They are no true knights, not one of them.

paragraphs.context: she saw Renly’s sword still in its scabbard, sheathed still
paragraphs.mainIdea: Renly is murdered by a living shadow: a gust of wind, his own shadow rising with a sword though his real sword is still sheathed, and his throat cut by a blade that is not there. Brienne is holding his body when the others burst in — so they will blame her.
paragraphs.simple: "I beg you in the name of the Mother," Catelyn began, when a sudden rush of wind threw open the door of the tent. She thought she saw something move, but when she turned her head, it was only the king's shadow moving against the silk walls. She heard Renly start a joke, his shadow moving, lifting its sword, black against green, the candles flickering and shaking — something was strange, wrong — and then she saw Renly's sword still in its sheath, still sheathed, but the shadow's sword …

paragraphs.context: even if they do not know it themselves yet.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn's cold realization as dawn comes: Renly's vast host — ten thousand lances with bright banners — now has no leader but Stannis. 'They belong to Stannis now, even if they do not know it themselves yet.' One shadow has won him everything.
paragraphs.simple: As the long fingers of dawn spread across the fields, color was returning to the world. Where grey men had sat on grey horses holding shadow spears, the points of ten thousand lances now shone cold and silver, and on the many flapping banners Catelyn saw the soft colors of red and pink and orange, the deep colors of blue and brown, the bright blaze of gold and yellow. All the power of Storm's End and Highgarden, the power that had been Renly's an hour ago. They belong to Stannis now, she realized, even if they do not know it themselves yet. Where else are they to turn, if not to the last Baratheon? Stannis has won everything with a single evil act.

paragraphs.context: as if he did not like what he’d smelled
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ghost refuses to enter the ringfort: he sniffs the gap in the stones and backs away. The wolf senses something wrong with this old place — and Ghost is never wrong about such things.
paragraphs.simple: But when they reached the ringfort, Ghost stopped again. He walked forward carefully to sniff at the gap in the stones, and then backed away, as if he did not like what he had smelled. Jon tried to grab him by the loose skin of his neck and drag him inside the ring with his bare hands — no easy job; the wolf weighed as much as Jon did, and was much stronger. "Ghost, what's wrong with you?" It was not like him to be so upset. In the end Jon had to give up. "As you wish," he told the wolf. "Go, hunt." The red eyes watched him as he walked back through the moss-covered stones.

paragraphs.context: He seized a handful and pulled it close to the torch
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ghost has found a buried cache: dragonglass daggers, spearheads, and arrowheads — the black stone that kills the Others — plus an old warhorn, all wrapped in a black Night's Watch cloak and buried recently. Someone meant these to be found.
paragraphs.simple: Under the dragonglass there was an old warhorn, made from the horn of a wild ox and bound with bronze. Jon shook the dirt out of it, and a stream of arrowheads fell out. He let them fall, and pulled up a corner of the cloth the weapons had been wrapped in, rubbing it between his fingers. Good wool, thick, a double weave, damp but not rotted. It could not have been in the ground for long. And it was dark. He took a handful and pulled it close to the torch. Not dark. Black.

paragraphs.context: It is the sea that comes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jojen's dream decoded: the 'sea' coming to Winterfell is not water — it is attackers from the sea, the ironborn. Bran hears it literally ('the sea is hundreds of leagues away'), but Jojen means reavers: 'the salt sea will flow over these walls' and drowned men will float in the yard.
paragraphs.simple: "It is the sea that comes."

paragraphs.context: It is his duty. Ser Rodrik is nothing if not dutiful
paragraphs.mainIdea: Theon's scheme: Dagmer will feint at Torrhen's Square — openly building siege engines he never means to use — so the 'dutiful' Ser Rodrik rides out of Winterfell with its garrison. 'It's not Torrhen's Square I mean to take.' The real target is left unsaid: Winterfell itself.
paragraphs.simple: "Leobald will not know that. When he sees you raising siege towers, his old woman's blood will run cold, and he will cry for help like a sheep. Hold back your archers, Uncle, and let the raven fly. The castellan at Winterfell is a brave man, but age has stiffened his wits as well as his limbs. When he learns that one of his king's bannermen is under attack by the fearsome Dagmer Cleftjaw, he will gather his strength and ride to Tallhart's aid. It is his duty. Ser Rodrik is nothing if not dutiful."
hardWords: his old woman's blood will run cold

paragraphs.context: his throat a red ruin, eyes gaping sightlessly
paragraphs.mainIdea: Weese is dead — throat torn out by his own spotted dog. The onlookers blame Harren's ghost, but Jaqen, leaning against the tower, lays two fingers against his cheek: one death paid, two still owed. Arya understands: 'It wasn't Harren. It was me.'
paragraphs.simple: A dozen people got there before her, though none of them was coming very close. Arya squeezed between them. Weese was lying spread out across the stones, his throat a red ruin, his eyes staring sightlessly up at a bank of grey cloud. His ugly spotted dog stood on his chest, licking at the blood pulsing from his neck, and every so often tearing a mouthful of flesh out of the dead man's face.

paragraphs.context: the king cut out Stafford Lannister’s heart and fed it to the wolf
paragraphs.mainIdea: Campfire rumor: some say Robb 'cut out Stafford Lannister's heart and fed it to the wolf.' Catelyn cuts it off sharply — 'My son is no savage.' The tale shows how the Young Wolf is turning into a monster in the stories men tell.
paragraphs.simple: "He never took it. He slipped around it in the night. They say the direwolf showed him the way, that Grey Wind of his. The beast sniffed out a goat track that wound down a narrow valley and up along under a ridge — a crooked and stony way, yet wide enough for men riding one by one. The Lannisters in their watchtowers never got even a glimpse of them." Rivers lowered his voice. "Some say that after the battle, the king cut out Stafford Lannister's heart and fed it to the wolf."

paragraphs.context: the man sounded nothing like me, and yet the oafs were raising the portcullis
paragraphs.mainIdea: Edmure explains the hanged men: they were Tyrion's four infiltrators, hidden among the hundred red cloaks — a thief, a poisoner, a mummer, and a murderer. The mummer used Edmure's own voice to order the gate opened. They were caught only because the real Edmure happened to be returning by boat.
paragraphs.simple: "False envoys," Edmure declared. "They promised me their peace and gave up their weapons, so I allowed them freedom of the castle, and for three nights they ate my meat and drank my mead while I talked with Ser Cleos. On the fourth night, they tried to free the Kingslayer." He pointed up. "That big brute killed two guards with nothing but those ham hands of his — caught them by the throats and smashed their skulls together — while that skinny lad beside him was opening Lannister's cell with a bit of wire, gods curse him. The one on the end was some sort of damned mummer. He used my own voice to order that the River Gate be opened. The guardsmen swear to it, Enger and Delp and Long Lew, all three. If you ask me, the man sounded nothing like me, and yet the fools were raising the portcullis all the same."

paragraphs.context: Cersei had managed to buy herself three hollow drums
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion is amused: Cersei has bought herself three sellsword brothers, the Kettleblacks — but Bronn secretly pays them too. They are 'three hollow drums': they make all the fierce booming sounds Cersei wants, 'but there was nothing inside.'
paragraphs.simple: Well, let her enjoy her plots. She was much sweeter when she thought she was outwitting him. The Kettleblacks would charm her, take her coin, and promise her anything she asked — and why not, when Bronn was matching every copper penny, coin for coin? Friendly rogues, all three; the brothers were in truth much better at lying than they had ever been at killing. Cersei had managed to buy herself three hollow drums; they would make all the fierce booming sounds she wanted, but there was nothing inside. It amused Tyrion no end.
hardWords: matching every copper penny, coin for coin

paragraphs.context: holding the corpse of her dead baby above her head
paragraphs.mainIdea: The riot's spark: a starving mother holds her dead baby over her head; Joffrey flings her a coin that bounces off the corpse and starts a brawl. Then she recognizes Cersei and screams 'Brotherfucker!' — the mob knows the queen's secret, and the city explodes.
paragraphs.simple: Halfway along the route, a wailing woman forced her way between two watchmen and ran out into the street in front of the king and his companions, holding the corpse of her dead baby above her head. It was blue and swollen, horrible to look at, but the real horror was the mother's eyes. Joffrey looked for a moment as if he meant to ride her down, but Sansa Stark leaned over and said something to him. The king fumbled in his purse, and threw the woman a silver coin. The coin bounced off the child and rolled away, under the legs of the gold cloaks and into the crowd, where a dozen men began to fight for it. The mother never once blinked. Her skinny arms were trembling from the dead weight of her son.

paragraphs.context: The night is dark and full of terrors, Davos
paragraphs.mainIdea: Stannis tells Davos plainly: 'Ser Cortnay will be dead within the day' — not in fair combat, but by Melisandre's flames. Davos understands with horror: 'Yet they require me to make them true.' He must smuggle the red woman in to do the killing.
paragraphs.simple: "So did my brother, the day before his death. The night is dark and full of terrors, Davos."

paragraphs.context: But if we are winning, why am I so afraid?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn is afraid even though her brother Edmure has won a battle. Her fear warns the reader that this "victory" may bring bad trouble later.
paragraphs.simple: Catelyn is thinking to herself. Her brother has won, but she is still afraid. "We are winning," she thinks. "Then why am I so afraid?" Something about the news troubles her.

paragraphs.context: a long deep shivery cry, a howl to wake the sleepers
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is a wolf dream: the "he" is Summer, Bran's direwolf, not Bran. His howl echoes the Night's Watch vow — "I am the horn that wakes the sleepers."
paragraphs.simple: He heard the sound again — a sharp metal sound, clink and scrape. It made him jump to his feet. His ears stood up and his tail went up. He howled — a long, deep, shaking cry, a cry to wake sleeping people. But the town made of piled stone was dark and still. It was a wet, quiet night, a night that drives men inside. The rain had stopped, but the men still hid from the wet air, sitting close together by their fires in their little stone houses.

paragraphs.context: “Smiths have strong arms and weak heads,” observed Theon.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Theon has had the smith Mikken killed for saying no to him. His cold joke is a warning to everyone else: obey me, or die too.
paragraphs.simple: "Blacksmiths have strong arms and weak heads," Theon said. He has just had the smith killed because the man would not obey him. "But if the rest of you serve me as well as you served Ned Stark, you will find me as kind a lord as you could wish for." He is not being kind — he is frightening them into obeying him.

paragraphs.context: Arya put her lips to his ear. “It’s Jaqen H’ghar.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya cleverly names Jaqen H'ghar himself. He promised to kill anyone she names, so now he must kill himself — or make a deal with her. This forces him to help free the northern prisoners.
paragraphs.simple: Arya moved her mouth close to his ear. "It is Jaqen H'ghar," she whispered. She names him. Jaqen promised to kill any person she names. Now he must kill himself — or agree to a deal with her. In this way she forces him to help her free the men from the north.

paragraphs.context: His cheeks grew fuller, his eyes closer; his nose hooked
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaqen changes his face by magic: his cheeks, eyes, nose, and hair all become different. He is a Faceless Man, who can wear new faces. That is why Arya later calls him "the stranger in Jaqen's clothes."
paragraphs.simple: "I do. My time is done." Jaqen moved his hand down over his face, from the top of his head to his chin. Where his hand went, his face changed. His cheeks got rounder. His eyes moved closer together. His nose bent into a hook. A scar appeared on his right cheek, where no scar had been before. Then he shook his head, and his long straight hair — half red, half white — melted away. Under it was a cap of short, tight black curls.

paragraphs.context: blue and cold, whispering as they reached for her
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Undying crowd around Dany, touching and biting her. They want to feed on her life and keep her there forever. She is helpless until Drogon burns them with fire.
paragraphs.simple: Then black wings beat at her head, and a scream of anger cut the dark blue air. Suddenly the strange sights were gone, torn away. Dany's gasp turned to fear. The Undying were all around her — blue and cold. They whispered as they reached for her, pulling, touching, tugging at her clothes. They touched her with their dry cold hands and twisted their fingers through her hair. All the strength had left her arms and legs. She could not move. Even her heart had stopped beating. She felt a hand on her bare chest, pinching her. Teeth found the soft skin of her throat. A mouth came down on one eye, licking, sucking, biting…

paragraphs.context: the Three Whores, because they’d be giving Lord Stannis such a lusty welcome
paragraphs.mainIdea: The soldiers gave the three big war machines a rude nickname, "the Three Whores." It is a dirty soldier joke — the machines will give Stannis's men a "lusty welcome" — not something to take as a fact.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion Lannister rode his horse slowly toward the Mud Gate. "Winterfell is nothing to you," he told himself. "Be glad the place has fallen, and think about your own walls." The gate was open. Inside, three great war machines stood side by side in the market square. They looked over the walls like three huge birds. Their throwing arms were made from the trunks of old oak trees, with iron bands around them to keep them from breaking. The city guards had named them the Three Whores, because they would be giving Lord Stannis's men such an eager welcome. Or so we hope.

paragraphs.context: had begun to go out of the world the day the last dragon died
