paragraphs.mainIdea: The pyromancer says magic started to leave the world the day the last dragon died — and now his spells are working better. The hint is that magic is coming back because dragons have been born again.
paragraphs.simple: "Oh, pardon. I was just remembering something old Wisdom Pollitor told me once, when I was a learner. I asked him why so many of our spells seemed not as strong as the old books said they should be. He said it was because magic had started to leave the world the day the last dragon died." His spells are working better now — because dragons are alive again.

paragraphs.context: “Mercy was for this morning,” said Theon.
paragraphs.mainIdea: "Mercy was for this morning" means Theon will show no more mercy. He has decided to kill the miller's two young sons and say their bodies are Bran's and Rickon's, to hide that the Stark boys escaped him.
paragraphs.simple: "Mercy was for this morning," Theon said. "It is better to be feared than laughed at." "Before they made me angry." He will show no kindness now. He has decided to kill the miller's two little boys and pretend their bodies are Bran's and Rickon's, so no one will know the Stark boys got away from him.

paragraphs.context: but the gods hate kinslayers, even when they kill unknowing
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bael killed his own son without knowing it, and it ruined his house. Killing one's own family is the worst crime — the gods hate it even when done by accident. And Ygritte adds that a singer's truth is not the same as fact.
paragraphs.simple: "Yes," she said, "but the gods hate people who kill their own family, even when they kill without knowing. When Lord Stark came back from the battle and his mother saw Bael's head on his spear, she threw herself off a tower in her sadness. Her son did not live long after her. One of his lords cut the skin off him and wore it as a coat."

paragraphs.context: It was as if her own body had betrayed her to Joffrey
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa has had her first period. In a panic she tries to burn the bloody sheets so no one will know — because once they know she is "a woman," she will be married to Joffrey and forced to sleep with him. She feels her body has betrayed her to him.
paragraphs.simple: In the end it took three people to pull her away. And it was all for nothing. The bed sheets were burnt, but by the time they carried her off, her legs were bloody again. It was as if her own body had given her away to Joffrey, raising a red flag for all the world to see.

paragraphs.context: “Robert? Robert was hunting. That was his custom.
paragraphs.mainIdea: "Robert was hunting" is Cersei's bitter joke. Whenever she was about to give birth, King Robert would leave the castle to "hunt" — meaning he went to sleep with other women instead of staying with his wife.
paragraphs.simple: "Robert? Robert was hunting. That was what he always did. Whenever my time to give birth was near, my royal husband would run off to the trees with his hunters and dogs. When he came back he would give me some animal skins or a deer's head — and I would give him a baby." She is really saying he went to be with other women.

paragraphs.context: Not always, came the silent shout. Not before the crow.
paragraphs.mainIdea: In Jon's wolf dream, a voice speaks from the weirwood tree that wears his brother's face: "Not before the crow." The "crow" is the three-eyed crow from Bran's dreams. The short broken lines are its mysterious speech, not normal talk.
paragraphs.simple: "Not always," came the quiet shout that made no sound. "Not before the crow." The tree's face did not always have three eyes — not before the crow came to it.

paragraphs.context: “Leave me as many arrows as you can spare, brothers.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Squire Dalbridge will stay behind alone and die, holding off the wildlings with his bow so the others can escape. His grim joke is that he will shoot the eagle spying on them — a skinchanger's eyes.
paragraphs.simple: The squire put his head down. "Leave me as many arrows as you can give, brothers." He touched his longbow. "And see that my little horse gets an apple when you are home. He has earned it, poor little animal." He will stay behind alone to hold off the wildlings with his bow, so the others can get away.

paragraphs.context: Theon Greyjoy has mounted their heads on the walls of Winterfell
paragraphs.mainIdea: Catelyn hears that Bran and Rickon are dead — their heads are said to be on Winterfell's walls. This grief is what drives her, that same night, to free Jaime Lannister in hopes of trading him for her daughters.
paragraphs.simple: "Bran and Rickon tried to run away, but they were caught at a mill by the Acorn Water. Theon Greyjoy has put their heads on the walls of Winterfell. Theon Greyjoy — who ate at my table since he was a boy of ten." "I have said it, gods forgive me. I have said it and made it true." She is telling the terrible news, and she blames herself for saying the words out loud.

paragraphs.context: the more he struggled, the tighter the cord constricted around his throat
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jaime tells how the Mad King murdered Rickard and Brandon Stark: Rickard was hung up and slowly roasted alive in his armor, while Brandon, chained by the neck, strangled himself trying to reach a sword to free his father. This is the story behind Jaime's hated name "Kingslayer."
paragraphs.simple: "The fire-men roasted Lord Rickard slowly, feeding the fire carefully to keep it hot and even. His cloak caught fire first, then his coat, and soon he wore nothing but metal and ash. Next he would start to cook, Aerys promised — unless his son could free him. Brandon tried, but the more he fought, the tighter the rope squeezed around his throat. In the end he killed himself by choking."

paragraphs.context: “Give me your sword.” Catelyn held out her hand.
paragraphs.mainIdea: "Give me your sword." Catelyn takes Brienne's sword — she means to free Jaime herself, against her son's orders, so she can exchange him for Sansa and Arya.
paragraphs.simple: "Give me your sword," Catelyn said. She held out her hand. She will take Brienne's sword and free Jaime Lannister herself, even though her son ordered otherwise — so she can trade Jaime for Sansa and Arya.

paragraphs.context: On their iron spikes atop the gatehouse, the heads waited.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The heads on spikes above the gate are not Bran's and Rickon's. They are the miller's two young sons, killed by Theon's men. Theon is passing them off as the Stark boys to hide his failure.
paragraphs.simple: On their iron points on top of the gatehouse, the heads waited. They are not really the heads of Bran and Rickon. They are the heads of the miller's two little boys, killed by Theon's men. Theon is lying, saying they are the Stark boys, to hide that he let the real boys escape.

paragraphs.context: for what was Stannis Baratheon, if not the Stranger come to judge them?
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Stranger is the Seven's god of death, with a half-human face. The frightened people light candles even to him — because Stannis, coming to take the city, feels like death itself coming to judge them.
paragraphs.simple: Sansa had never seen the holy house so full of people, or so brightly lit. Great lines of rainbow-colored sunlight fell through the crystals in the high windows. Candles burned on every side, their little flames shining like stars. The Mother's and the Warrior's altars swam in light, but the Smith, the Crone, the Maid, and the Father had their worshipers too. And there were even a few flames dancing below the Stranger's half-human face — for what was Stannis Baratheon, if not the Stranger come to judge them? Sansa went to each of the Seven in turn, lit a candle at each altar, and then sat down on the benches between a thin old washerwoman and a boy no older than Rickon, dressed in the fine shirt of a knight's son. The old woman's hand was thin and hard, the boy's small and soft — but it was good to hold someone's hand. The air was hot and heavy, smelling of sweet smoke and sweat. It made her head spin to breathe it.

paragraphs.context: “To deal with treason, and to defend us if need be.
paragraphs.mainIdea: "To deal with treason" is Cersei's cold way of saying it. Ser Ilyn, the king's executioner, waits in the ballroom: if the city falls, he will behead the noblewomen — including Sansa — rather than let Stannis's men take them.
paragraphs.simple: The queen looked at the silent executioner. "To deal with treason, and to keep us safe if need be. He was a knight before he was an executioner." She pointed her spoon toward the end of the hall, where the tall wooden doors had been shut and locked. "When the axes break down those doors, you may be glad he is here."

paragraphs.context: the weapons of honest men, he told himself
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos remembers that Melisandre gave birth to a living shadow in the dark under Storm's End — a shadow thing that murdered Ser Cortnay Penrose. He is glad she is not at this battle and wants no part of her or her god.
paragraphs.simple: He could not look at the burning-heart flag without thinking of the shadow Melisandre had given birth to in the dark under Storm's End. "At least we fight this battle in daylight, with the weapons of honest men," he told himself. The red woman and her dark children would have no part of it. Stannis had sent her back to Dragonstone with his nephew Edric Storm, who was born outside marriage. His captains had said a battlefield was no place for a woman. Only the queen's men had disagreed, and not loudly. Still, the king had almost said no to them — until Lord Bryce Caron said, "Your Grace, if the sorceress is with us, afterward men will say it was her victory, not yours. They will say you owe your crown to her spells." That had changed everything. Davos himself had said nothing during the quarrel, but if truth be told, he had not been sad to see her go. He wanted no part of Melisandre or her god.

paragraphs.context: his maimed hand to clutch at the leather pouch that held his fingerbones
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos holds the leather bag with his finger bones — his luck charm. Stannis once cut off his finger joints as punishment for smuggling, and Davos has kept the bones for luck ever since.
paragraphs.simple: "No," he said. "No, NOOOOOO!" Above the roar and crash of battle, no one heard him but Matthos. The captain of the Swordfish did not hear him either — he was busy trying to stab something at last with his clumsy fat sword. The Swordfish went to battle speed. Davos lifted his hurt hand to hold tight the little leather bag that carried his finger bones. It was his luck charm: Stannis had once cut off the ends of his fingers as punishment for smuggling, and Davos had kept the bones for luck ever since.

paragraphs.context: The chain. Gods save us, they’ve raised the chain.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion's giant harbor chain has been raised across the mouth of the Blackwater. Stannis's ships are trapped: wildfire burning behind them, and a wall of hot chain ahead. "The mouth of the Blackwater Rush had turned into the mouth of hell."
paragraphs.simple: "The chain. Gods save us, they have raised the chain." Tyrion's great iron chain has been pulled up across the mouth of the river. Stannis's ships cannot get out.

paragraphs.context: He is afraid, Tyrion realized, shocked. The Hound is frightened.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Hound is terrified of fire — he was badly burned as a boy. Seeing the wildfire, his courage breaks; he refuses Tyrion's order and runs from the battle. His fear is stronger than his duty.
paragraphs.simple: "He is afraid," Tyrion realized, shocked. The Hound is frightened. He tried to explain what they needed. "They have brought a battering ram to the gate — you can hear them. We need to scatter them—" But the Hound would not move. Fire terrifies him: he was badly burned as a child. His courage has broken, and he will not obey.

paragraphs.context: I do not mean for him to have us alive.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei tells Sansa the truth about Ser Ilyn: if Stannis takes the city, she will have the executioner kill all the noblewomen. "I do not mean for him to have us alive." She would rather they die than be taken.
paragraphs.simple: "He is here for us, he says," the queen said. "Stannis may take the city and he may take the throne, but I will not let him judge me. I do not mean for him to have us alive." If Stannis wins, Cersei will have the executioner kill all the noblewomen — including Sansa — rather than let them be taken.

paragraphs.context: Battle fever. I am half a man and drunk with slaughter
paragraphs.mainIdea: "Battle fever" is the strange joy some fighters feel in battle: fear and thought go away, time slows, and only the fight is left. Tyrion, who never thought he would feel it, is "drunk with slaughter."
paragraphs.simple: The battle fever. He had never thought he would feel it himself, though Jaime had told him about it often. How time seemed to blur and slow and even stop. How the past and the future went away, until there was nothing but this moment. How fear went away, and thought went away, and even your body. "You don't feel your wounds then, or the pain in your back from the heavy armor, or the sweat running down into your eyes. You stop feeling, you stop thinking, you stop being you. There is only the fight, the enemy, this man and then the next and the next and the next. And you know they are afraid and tired, but you are not. You are alive. Death is all around you, but their swords move so slowly you can dance through them, laughing." Battle fever. "I am half a man and drunk with killing — let them kill me if they can!"

paragraphs.context: Ser Mandon was holding out his left hand, why…
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ser Mandon Moore, a Kingsguard, tries to murder Tyrion in the fighting: he holds out his left hand to help — a swordsman offering the wrong hand — then cuts Tyrion's face with his sword. Someone knocks Mandon into the water; Tyrion thinks the voice sounds like Pod's.
paragraphs.simple: There on the deck of the next ship, across a widening stretch of black water, stood Ser Mandon Moore, with a hand held out. Yellow and green fire shone on the white of his armor. His metal glove was sticky with blood, but Tyrion reached for it anyway, wishing his arms were longer. Only at the very last, as their fingers touched across the gap, something worried him… Ser Mandon was holding out his left hand. Why… A swordsman would offer his right. It was a trap: Mandon meant to cut him.

paragraphs.context: a wetness that was not blood
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Hound, drunk and hopeless, begs Sansa for a song, then holds a knife to her. She sings a hymn, and softly touches his burned cheek — "a wetness that was not blood" (tears). He leaves his white cloak: he is done playing the true knight.
paragraphs.simple: Something made her lift her hand and hold his cheek with her fingers. The room was too dark for her to see him, but she could feel the stickiness of the blood — and a wetness that was not blood. Tears. "Little bird," he said once more, his voice rough and harsh like steel on stone. Then he stood up from the bed. Sansa heard cloth tearing, then the softer sound of footsteps going away. He left his white cloak behind: he is done pretending to be a true knight.

paragraphs.context: Lord Renly in his green armor, with the fires shimmering off his golden antlers
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dontos swears he saw the dead Lord Renly leading the attack in his green armor — but Renly was murdered earlier in the book. It must be someone else wearing Renly's armor to frighten Stannis's men, who loved Renly.
paragraphs.simple: "It was Lord Renly! Lord Renly in his green armor, with the fires shining off his golden antlers! Lord Renly with his tall spear in his hand! They say he killed Ser Guyard Morrigen himself in single combat, and a dozen other great knights as well. It was Renly, it was Renly, it was Renly! Oh! The flags, dear Sansa! Oh! To be a knight!" But Renly was murdered earlier. It cannot really be him — someone else must be wearing his armor to frighten Stannis's men, who loved Renly.

paragraphs.context: There was a manticore in that jewel box he gave me
paragraphs.mainIdea: The "gift" box held a manticore, a deadly poisonous creature — a killing try by a Sorrowful Man. The old man Arstan knocked it out of her hand and saved Dany. He and Belwas were sent by Magister Illyrio of Pentos.
paragraphs.simple: "They were defending me." Dany shook her hand to shake off the sting. "It was the other one, the man from Qarth." When she looked around, he was gone. "He was a Sorrowful Man. There was a manticore in that jewel box he gave me. This man knocked it out of my hand." The brass merchant was still rolling on the ground. She went to him and helped him stand up. "Were you stung?"

paragraphs.context: free for the use of any man who wanted them
paragraphs.mainIdea: The gentle words "shared their favors" and "free for the use of any man" hide a brutal fact: the women are being raped by the soldiers. Arya hears it all as she goes about her work.
paragraphs.simple: The new rulers of Harrenhal are punishing everyone who helped the Lannisters. Tothmure the raven-master is sent to be beheaded because he sent birds to Casterly Rock and King's Landing. Lucan the armorer is killed for making weapons for the Lannisters. Goodwife Harra is killed for telling the castle servants to wait on them. The steward is killed for handing Lord Tywin the keys to the money room. The cook lives, and people joke it is because he made the weasel soup. But poor Pia and the other women who slept with Lannister soldiers get a cruel punishment: stocks are built for them. They are stripped and shaved, and left in the middle courtyard by the bear pit, where any man may use their bodies freely. This is rape, dressed up in polite words.

paragraphs.context: It’s not true, it can’t be true, it’s just some Lannister lie
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya has just heard that Bran and Rickon are dead and Winterfell is lost. She refuses to believe it and calls it a Lannister lie. Her hope is wrong: Winterfell really has fallen.
paragraphs.simple: For a moment Arya forgets to breathe. Bran and Rickon dead? What does this man mean about Winterfell? Joffrey could never take Winterfell, never. Robb would never allow it. Then she remembers: Robb is not at Winterfell. He is far away in the west, and Bran is crippled, and Rickon is only four years old. She uses all her strength to stay still and quiet, the way Syrio Forel taught her, standing like a piece of furniture. She feels tears filling her eyes and forces them back. It is not true, it cannot be true, it is just some Lannister lie.

paragraphs.context: It is a fine thing to have so many valiant brothers
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bolton is not agreeing with the Freys. His smile and his praise of "so many valiant brothers" is a polite dismissal. He has no plan to follow their advice; he is sending them away.
paragraphs.simple: "And who will tell him so?" Roose Bolton smiled. "It is a fine thing to have so many brave brothers in such troubled times. I shall think about everything you have said." Bolton sounds polite and grateful, but his pretty words mean the opposite: he is brushing the Freys aside. He will not do what they advise.

paragraphs.context: take the place of your dear Domeric and rule the Dreadfort
paragraphs.mainIdea: Walda's letter is always the same sweet formula, but one line hides a death: "take the place of your dear Domeric" means Bolton's trueborn son Domeric is dead, and Walda promises to give him new sons.
paragraphs.simple: Lady Walda writes to Bolton from the Twins almost every day, but all her letters say the same thing. "I pray for you morning, noon, and night, my sweet lord," she writes, "and I count the days until you share my bed again. Come back to me soon, and I will give you many trueborn sons to take the place of your dear Domeric and rule the Dreadfort after you." Behind the sweet words is a sad fact: Domeric, Bolton's trueborn son, is dead, and Walda is promising him new sons. Arya pictures a fat pink baby in a cradle, covered with fat pink leeches.

paragraphs.context: where the queen had made her father kill Sansa’s wolf
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya is glad Darry castle will burn because she remembers it from the first book: after her fight with Joffrey, the queen made her father kill Sansa's wolf Lady at Darry. That is why she thinks the place deserves to burn.
paragraphs.simple: Arya was glad to hear that the castle of the Darrys would be burned. That was the place they had brought her when she was caught after her fight with Joffrey, and where the queen had made her father kill Sansa's wolf. It deserves to burn. But she wished that Robett Glover and Ser Helman Tallhart would come back to Harrenhal; they had marched away too quickly, before she had been able to decide whether to trust them with her secret.

paragraphs.context: the lone wolf dies, but the pack survives
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arya hears a wolf howl and then seems to hear her father's voice speaking his saying about the pack. Ned is dead; this is her memory of him, not a ghost. The words give her strength to choose who she is.
paragraphs.simple: For a long moment there was no sound but the wind and the water and the creak of leaf and branch. And then, far far away, beyond the godswood and the haunted towers and the huge stone walls of Harrenhal, from somewhere out in the world, came the long lonely howl of a wolf. Goosebumps rose on Arya's skin, and for a moment she felt dizzy. Then, very faintly, it seemed as if she heard her father's voice. "When the snows fall and the white winds blow, the lone wolf dies, but the pack survives," he said. Her father is dead, so this is only her memory of his voice — but his words give her strength to remember who she is.

paragraphs.context: Lord Paramount of the Trident, Sansa thought, and Lord of Harrenhal
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa thinks Littlefinger's new titles are empty: Harrenhal is cursed and held by others, and the river lords will never follow him. She misses the danger: the title "Lord Paramount of the Trident" is a huge step up for a schemer like him.
paragraphs.simple: Joffrey laughed, and the court laughed with him. Lord Paramount of the Trident, Sansa thought, and Lord of Harrenhal as well. She did not understand why that should make Littlefinger so happy; the honors were as empty as the title given to Hallyne the Pyromancer. Everyone knew Harrenhal was cursed, and the Lannisters did not even hold it right now. Besides, the lords of the Trident were sworn to Riverrun and House Tully, and to the King in the North; they would never accept Littlefinger as their liege lord. Unless they are made to. Unless my brother and my uncle and my grandfather are all thrown down and killed. The thought made Sansa anxious, but she told herself she was being silly. Robb has beaten them every time. He'll beat Lord Baelish too, if he must.

paragraphs.context: queen whore and king worm, vile dwarf and whispering spider, the false flowers
paragraphs.mainIdea: The shouting knight's insults each name a real person: the "queen whore" is Cersei, the "king worm" is Joffrey, the "vile dwarf" is Tyrion, the "whispering spider" is Varys (called the Spider), and the "false flowers" are the Tyrells, whose sign is the rose.
paragraphs.simple: The knight raised his voice instead. "Joffrey is the black worm eating the heart of the realm! Darkness was his father, and death his mother! Destroy him before he corrupts you all! Destroy them all, queen whore and king worm, vile dwarf and whispering spider, the false flowers. Save yourselves!" One of the gold cloaks knocked the man off his feet, but he kept shouting. "The scouring fire will come! King Stannis will return!" His insults are code names: the "queen whore" is Cersei, the "king worm" is Joffrey, the "vile dwarf" is Tyrion, the "whispering spider" is Varys, who is called the Spider, and the "false flowers" are the Tyrells, whose sign is the rose.

paragraphs.context: They say the Iron Throne can be perilous cruel to those
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sansa recalls the saying that the Iron Throne hurts kings who were not meant to sit it. Joffrey has just cut himself on one of its blades while raging, and she takes it as a sign the old saying is true of him.
paragraphs.simple: The light outside the windows was fading by the time the court session drew to a close. Sansa felt weak with exhaustion as she walked down from the gallery. She wondered how badly Joffrey had cut himself. People say the Iron Throne can be cruelly dangerous to those who were not meant to sit on it. Joffrey has just cut himself on one of its swords, and Sansa takes it as a sign that the old saying is true of him.

paragraphs.context: Done with you? They’ve scarcely begun
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dontos is crushing Sansa's joy: being set aside as Joffrey's bride does not free her. She is still a valuable hostage the queen will never release, and as king Joffrey could still force himself on her, fathering bastards instead of trueborn sons.
paragraphs.simple: He took her hand. "Oh, Jonquil, my poor Jonquil, you do not understand. Done with you? They've scarcely begun." Dontos is killing Sansa's hope. Being set aside as Joffrey's bride does not make her free. She is still a precious hostage that the queen will never let go — and Joffrey, as king, could still force himself on her and father bastards on her instead of trueborn sons.

paragraphs.context: It’s magic, you see. It’s justice you hold. It’s vengeance for your father
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dontos talks in riddles about the hair net: "magic," "justice," "vengeance for your father," "home." He will not explain plainly. Sansa only wants a ship to escape on, not jewelry, and does not yet grasp that the net matters more than it looks.
paragraphs.simple: "Lovelier than you know, sweet child. It's magic, you see. It's justice you hold. It's vengeance for your father." Dontos leaned close and kissed her again. "It's home." Dontos talks in riddles about the hair net. He calls it magic, justice, vengeance for her father, home — but he will not say plainly what he means. Sansa only wants a ship to escape King's Landing on, not jewelry, and she does not yet understand that the net is far more important than it looks.

paragraphs.context: The small grey man was unafraid. “My order serves.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Luwin is stating his maester's oath: he serves the castle and the realm, not one man. Whoever holds Winterfell, even Theon, he is bound to give honest counsel. That is why he urges Theon to yield.
paragraphs.simple: The small grey man was unafraid. "My order serves." Luwin is a maester, and maesters swear an oath: they serve the castle and the realm, not any one man. Whoever holds Winterfell — even Theon — Luwin must give him honest counsel. That is why he is urging Theon to give up.

paragraphs.context: It’s not victory he wants, it’s an end worthy of a song
paragraphs.mainIdea: Black Lorren does not want victory; he wants a glorious death. For the ironborn, dying heroically in battle is "an end worthy of a song." Theon understands this and refuses him.
paragraphs.simple: He means to die, thought Theon. It's not victory he wants, it's an end worthy of a song. "We'll use the noose." Black Lorren does not want to win; he wants to die gloriously in battle. For the ironborn, a hero's death is the finest end — one that singers will sing about. Theon understands what Lorren truly wants, and he refuses to give it to him.
hardWords: an end worthy of a song

paragraphs.context: A black cloak can’t be turned. I’d be as good as any man…
paragraphs.mainIdea: Theon is daydreaming, not planning. The Night's Watch means no crown, no sons, no wife, and hard service — not becoming Lord Commander with his own ship and wildling lovers. His fantasy shows he still does not grasp what the black really costs.
paragraphs.simple: I have plenty of black clothes, once I tear the krakens off. Even my horse is black. I could rise high in the Watch — chief of rangers, likely even Lord Commander. Let Asha keep the bloody islands, they're as dreary as she is. If I served at Eastwatch, I could command my own ship, and there's fine hunting beyond the Wall. As for women, what wildling woman wouldn't want a prince in her bed? A slow smile crept across his face. A black cloak can't be turned. I'd be as good as any man… Theon is not really planning; he is dreaming. Joining the Night's Watch means no crown, no sons, no wife, and a life of hard service — not glory, ships, and lovers. His fantasy shows he still does not understand what the black truly costs.
hardWords: A black cloak can't be turned

paragraphs.context: I am saved, Theon thought. So why did he feel so empty
paragraphs.mainIdea: Theon thinks he is saved, but the reader should feel dread, not relief. The "friends" from the Dreadfort are Ramsay Snow's men, and within the hour they will turn on him and burn Winterfell.
paragraphs.simple: I am saved, Theon thought. So why did he feel so empty? This was victory, sweet victory, the deliverance he had prayed for. He glanced at Maester Luwin. To think how close I came to yielding, and taking the black… Theon believes he is rescued — but the reader should feel dread, not relief. The "friends" from the Dreadfort are Ramsay Snow's men, and within the hour they will turn on Theon and burn Winterfell.

paragraphs.context: And now, my sweet prince, there was a woman promised me
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the chapter's great reveal: the man is not Reek the servant but Ramsay Snow, the Bastard of Bolton. He swapped clothes with Reek so the real Reek died in his place. "Snow" is the surname given to northern bastards; he now demands to be called Bolton.
paragraphs.simple: The man laughed. "The wretch is dead." He stepped closer and told his story: when the riders came, he gave his horse and his fine clothes — calfskin boots, velvet doublet, silver-chased swordbelt, even his sable cloak — to his servant Reek, and told him to ride for the Dreadfort for help. He dressed himself in Reek's rags and smeared himself with filth. When the arrow went through Reek's back, everyone thought the dead man was Ramsay. Now the truth comes out: this man is not Reek the servant. He is Ramsay Snow, the Bastard of Bolton, and he has brought his father's own garrison to Winterfell. "Snow" is the surname given to northern bastards; now he demands to be called Bolton.

paragraphs.context: Smooth seamless skin covered his teeth. The discovery terrified him
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the fever dream Tyrion finds he has no mouth — smooth skin where his lips should be. It is dream-logic for feeling voiceless and powerless, and it foreshadows the truth: his face is badly wounded and wrapped in bandages.
paragraphs.simple: He would have asked one of the silent sisters, but when he tried to speak he found he had no mouth. Smooth seamless skin covered his teeth. The discovery terrified him. How could he live without a mouth? He began to run. The city was not far. He would be safe inside the city, away from all these dead. He did not belong with the dead. He had no mouth, but he was still a living man. No, a lion, a lion, and alive. But when he reached the city walls, the gates were shut against him. This is a fever dream. Having no mouth is dream-logic for feeling voiceless and powerless — and it hints at the truth: his face is badly wounded and wrapped in bandages.

paragraphs.context: He dreamed of a better place, a snug little cottage by the sunset sea
paragraphs.mainIdea: This long remembered scene is Tyrion's memory of Tysha, the girl he married and loved when young. The sweet memory curdles at the end: he now believes she was only a whore paid by Jaime, so every tender word feels like a lie.
paragraphs.simple: He dreamed of a better place, a snug little cottage by the sunset sea. The walls were crooked and cracked and the floor was made of packed earth, but he had always been warm there, even when they let the fire go out. She used to tease him about never feeding the fire — that had always been a servant's task. "We have no servants," she would remind him, and he would say, "You have me, I'm your servant," and she would say, "A lazy servant. What do they do with lazy servants in Casterly Rock, my lord?" and he would tell her, "They kiss them." That always made her giggle. "They do not neither. They beat them, I bet," she would say, but he would insist, "No, they kiss them, just like this," and he would show her how — kissing her fingers, her wrists, her elbows, her funny ears, her cheeks, her nose with the little bump, her sweet brows, her hair, her lips, her mouth. This is Tyrion's memory of Tysha, the girl he married and loved when he was young. But the sweet memory is poisoned now: he believes she was only a whore paid by Jaime, so every tender word feels like a lie.

paragraphs.context: “Own bed. Own chambers.” Where I will have my own men about me
paragraphs.mainIdea: "I'll wager she did" is sarcasm. Cersei claims she kept Tyrion close so she could watch over him herself; Tyrion does not believe her care is loving. He suspects she wants him where she can control him — or finish him.
paragraphs.simple: I'll wager she did. "Return me," Tyrion commanded. "Own bed. Own chambers." Where I will have my own men about me, and my own maester too, if I find one I can trust. Cersei claims she kept Tyrion close in her own care so she could look after him. Tyrion's "I'll wager she did" is sarcasm — he does not believe her for a moment. He suspects she wants him close so she can control him, or so she can finish him off.

paragraphs.context: The smallfolk say it was King Renly’s ghost, but wiser men know better
paragraphs.mainIdea: The smallfolk believe King Renly's ghost saved the city. The truth, as Ballabar tells it, is ordinary: Lord Tywin and the Tyrells arrived in time. The ghost story shows how frightened common people turn victory into legend.
paragraphs.simple: "Since the night of the battle. Lord Tywin saved us all. The smallfolk say it was King Renly's ghost, but wiser men know better. It was your father and Lord Tyrell, with the Knight of Flowers and Lord Littlefinger. They rode through the ashes and took the usurper Stannis in the rear. It was a great victory, and now Lord Tywin has settled into the Tower of the Hand to help His Grace set the realm to rights, gods be praised." The common people believe King Renly's ghost saved the city. The plain truth is that Lord Tywin and the Tyrells arrived in time. The ghost story shows how frightened ordinary people turn a victory into a legend.

paragraphs.context: Night gathers, and now my watch begins. It shall not end until my death
paragraphs.mainIdea: These are the vows of the Night's Watch, which Jon swore for life. Every line binds him: no wife, no lands, no children, no glory. Qhorin is about to order him to seem to break these vows, which is why Jon makes him swear to tell Mormont the truth.
paragraphs.simple: "If you like." Their voices blended as one beneath the rising moon, while Ghost listened and the mountains themselves bore witness. "Night gathers, and now my watch begins. It shall not end until my death. I shall take no wife, hold no lands, father no children. I shall wear no crowns and win no glory. I shall live and die at my post. I am the sword in the darkness. I am the watcher on the walls. I am the fire that burns against the cold, the light that brings the dawn, the horn that wakes the sleepers, the shield that guards the realms of men. I pledge my life and honor to the Night's Watch, for this night and all the nights to come." These are the vows of the Night's Watch, which Jon swore for life. Every line binds him: no wife, no lands, no children, no glory. Qhorin is about to order Jon to pretend to break these vows, which is why Jon makes Qhorin swear to tell Mormont the truth.

paragraphs.context: “They warned me bastard blood was craven,” he heard Qhorin
paragraphs.mainIdea: Qhorin's cold insult — "bastard blood was craven," "Run to your new masters, coward" — is an act. He is playing the betrayed commander so the wildlings will believe Jon's defection is real. Jon's reddening face is real shame at hearing it.
paragraphs.simple: "They warned me bastard blood was craven," he heard Qhorin Halfhand say coldly behind him. "I see it is so. Run to your new masters, coward." Qhorin's cruel insult is an act. He is playing the part of the betrayed commander so the wildlings will believe that Jon's defection to them is real. Jon's face turns red with real shame as he hears it.

paragraphs.context: “The bird hates you, Jon Snow,” said Ygritte. “And well he might.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The eagle hates Jon for a reason: it is a skinchanger. The bird was the wildling Orell, whom Jon killed in the pass; Orell's spirit passed into his eagle at death. That is why it screams at Jon and shadows the rangers.
paragraphs.simple: "The bird hates you, Jon Snow," said Ygritte. "And well he might. He was a man, before you killed him." The eagle hates Jon for a reason: it is a skinchanger's second body. The bird was the wildling Orell, whom Jon killed in the pass; when Orell died, his spirit passed into his eagle. That is why the eagle screams at Jon and follows the rangers.

paragraphs.context: he could see the great piles of man-rock stark against the swirling flames
paragraphs.mainIdea: The chapter opens inside Summer the direwolf's mind, not Bran's. That is why men's things get wolf names: "man-rock" is stone buildings, "man-claws" are swords, "hardskin" is armor, the "man-pack" is a group of humans.
paragraphs.simple: He padded over dry needles and brown leaves, to the edge of the wood where the pines grew thin. Beyond the open fields he could see the great piles of man-rock stark against the swirling flames. The wind blew hot and rich with the smell of blood and burnt meat, so strong he began to slaver. This is not Bran thinking — we are inside the mind of Summer, his direwolf. That is why human things get wolf names: "man-rock" means stone buildings, "man-claws" mean swords, "hardskin" means armor, and the "man-pack" means a group of humans.

paragraphs.context: “The wolf ate,” Jojen said. “Not you. Take care, Bran.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jojen is warning Bran: "Remember who you are." Bran is spending so long inside Summer's skin that he forgets his human body — he even thinks he ate the elk, when only the wolf ate. If he stays too long, he may lose himself.
paragraphs.simple: "The wolf ate," Jojen said. "Not you. Take care, Bran. Remember who you are." Jojen is warning Bran. Bran spends so long inside Summer's skin that he forgets his human body — he even thinks he ate the elk, when only the wolf ate. If he stays inside the wolf too long, he may lose himself and never come back.

paragraphs.context: the clothes fit, but the muscles in his legs… poor lad…
paragraphs.mainIdea: Luwin worked out that the burned boys were not Bran and Rickon. The clothes fit, but the leg muscles were wrong: Bran's legs are withered from his fall, while the corpses had the strong legs of healthy miller's boys.
paragraphs.simple: "The legs, I could tell… the clothes fit, but the muscles in his legs… poor lad…" He coughed, and blood came up from inside him. "You vanished… in the woods… how, though?" Dying Luwin explains how he knew the burned boys were not Bran and Rickon. The clothes fit, but the leg muscles were wrong: Bran's legs are withered from his fall, while the corpses had the strong legs of healthy miller's boys.

paragraphs.context: “Listen,” Luwin said to Osha, “the princes… Robb’s heirs.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Luwin's dying counsel is to split the two princes up: "Not together." As Robb's heirs, they are safer apart — if one is caught or killed, the other may still live.
paragraphs.simple: "Listen," Luwin said to Osha, "the princes… Robb's heirs. Not… not together… do you hear?" Luwin's dying counsel is to split the two princes up: not together. As Robb's heirs, Bran and Rickon are safer apart — if one is caught or killed, the other may still live.

paragraphs.context: “I beg…” The maester swallowed. “… a… a drink of water, and…
paragraphs.mainIdea: The "boon" Luwin begs for is a quick death. He is dying in pain and asks Osha to end it for him. She sends the children away first, and grants it off-page: "She said no word of Maester Luwin."
paragraphs.simple: "I beg…" The maester swallowed. "… a… a drink of water, and… another boon. If you would…" The "boon" — the favor — that Luwin begs for is a quick death. He is dying in pain and asks Osha to end it for him. She sends the children away first, and grants his wish off the page: afterward, "she said no word of Maester Luwin."

paragraphs.context: It was not dead, just broken. Like me, he thought. I’m not dead either
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran's closing thought is the chapter's theme: Winterfell is "not dead, just broken. Like me." The burned castle mirrors his own broken body — ruined, but still standing and still himself.
paragraphs.simple: At the edge of the wolfswood, Bran turned in his basket for one last glimpse of the castle that had been his life. Wisps of smoke still rose into the grey sky, but no more than might have risen from Winterfell's chimneys on a cold autumn afternoon. Soot stains marked some of the arrow loops, and here and there a crack or a missing merlon could be seen in the curtain wall, but it seemed little enough from this distance. The tops of the keeps and towers still stood as they had for hundreds of years, and it was hard to tell that the castle had been sacked and burned at all. The stone is strong, Bran told himself, the roots of the trees go deep, and under the ground the Kings of Winter sit their thrones. So long as those remained, Winterfell remained. It was not dead, just broken. Like me, he thought. I'm not dead either. The burned castle mirrors Bran's own broken body — ruined, but still standing and still himself.

paragraphs.context: the only lord in the Seven Kingdoms who could field an army
paragraphs.mainIdea: "The Late Lord Frey" is a mocking nickname with a double meaning: at the battle on the Trident the Freys arrived late, after the fighting was done. The joke that he could "field an army out of his breeches" means he has so many children and grandchildren they alone could make an army.
paragraphs.simple: Powerful, wealthy, and numerous, the Freys are bannermen to House Tully, their swords sworn to the service of Riverrun, but they have not always been diligent in performing their duty. When Robert Baratheon met Rhaegar Targaryen on the Trident, the Freys did not arrive until the battle was done, and thereafter Lord Hoster Tully always called Lord Walder "the Late Lord Frey." Lord Frey agreed to support the cause of the King in the North only after Robb Stark agreed to a betrothal, promising to marry one of his daughters or granddaughters after the war was done. Lord Walder has known ninety-one name days, but only recently took his eighth wife, a girl seventy years his junior. It is said of him that he is the only lord in the Seven Kingdoms who could field an army out of his breeches. "The Late Lord Frey" is a mocking nickname: the Freys came late to the battle, and "late" also hints at being dead. The breeches joke means he has so many children and grandchildren that they alone could form an army.

paragraphs.context: they do honor to all kings and obey none
paragraphs.mainIdea: This states the Night's Watch rule of neutrality: the Watch takes no part in the wars for the throne. "They do honor to all kings and obey none" means they respect every claimant but serve none of them.
paragraphs.simple: The Night's Watch protects the realm, and is sworn to take no part in civil wars and contests for the throne. Traditionally, in times of rebellion, they do honor to all kings and obey none. This is the Watch's rule of neutrality: they fight the enemies beyond the Wall, not the wars between kings. They respect every claimant to the throne but serve none of them.

sentences.context: My fingers will grow back before that man bends
sentences.simple: Stannis is so proud that my cut-off fingers will grow back before he ever listens to reason — that is, never.
sentences.grammar: An impossible event (fingers growing back) placed first in a comparison to mean the second event will never happen.

sentences.context: Would that my fears could vanish so easily
sentences.simple: I wish my fears could disappear as easily as that ship disappeared behind the headland.
sentences.grammar: "Would that" is an old-fashioned way of saying "I wish"; the wish that follows stays in the plain verb form.

sentences.context: A clever fool and a foolish wise man
sentences.simple: Melisandre's riddle: Patchface is a fool who speaks hidden truths, while Cressen is a wise man about to do something foolish.
sentences.grammar: A fragment built on crossed opposites: two noun phrases, each pairing an adjective with the opposite meaning of its noun.

sentences.context: Old he might be, yet he was still
sentences.simple: He might be old, but he was still a learned maester trained at the Citadel.
sentences.grammar: Inversion for emphasis: the adjective "old" is fronted before the verb; the normal order would be "He might be old."

sentences.context: the old king, Aerys II Targaryen, who had not been quite
sentences.simple: The king — the old king, Aerys II Targaryen, who had not yet gone as mad as he later would — had sent Lord Steffon to find a bride for Prince Rhaegar, who had no sisters to marry.
sentences.grammar: A parenthetical explanation set off by em dashes: the clause between the dashes names which king is meant and can be removed without breaking the sentence.

sentences.context: The night is dark and full of terrors
sentences.simple: Melisandre's prayer: the night is dark and full of terrors — full of frightening things.
sentences.grammar: A fixed religious formula where "terrors" is a noun meaning "frightening things," not an adjective.

sentences.context: Once I might have silenced him forever, but now
sentences.simple: Cressen thinks: once I could have had him killed quietly, but now it is too late — and his thought trails off unfinished.
sentences.grammar: Euphemism plus ellipsis: "silenced him forever" means "had him killed," and the sentence breaks off with "…" leaving the ending unsaid.

sentences.context: It wasn't him as killed your father, girl, nor that
sentences.simple: It was not he who killed your father, girl, and neither did that thieving Lommy.
sentences.grammar: Dialect double negative: "as" stands in for "who," and "nor … neither" still adds up to a single negative in Yoren's speech.

sentences.context: You'd be one knight the poorer
sentences.simple: You would lose a knight — you would have one knight fewer.
sentences.grammar: "The + noun + the + comparative" used elliptically: "one knight the poorer" means "poorer by one knight."

sentences.context: with a black beard; you'll recall him if you try
sentences.simple: Tyrion is sarcastic: your father was a large fierce man with a black beard — surely even you remember him. He is mocking Joffrey, who of course remembers his own father.
sentences.grammar: Sarcasm through understatement: a painfully obvious description is presented as a helpful reminder.

sentences.context: A lady's armor is courtesy, that was it
sentences.simple: Septa Mordane's lesson: a lady's armor is courtesy — politeness protects a lady the way armor protects a knight. Sansa finally remembers the saying.
sentences.grammar: Metaphor as definition: "armor" is equated with "courtesy," and "that was it" marks the moment of remembering.

sentences.context: As loyal as a deer surrounded by wolves
sentences.simple: Tyrion does not believe her: as "loyal" as a deer surrounded by wolves — a deer only pretends friendship with wolves out of fear.
sentences.grammar: Ironic simile: the "as … as" comparison means the opposite of loyalty, since a deer among wolves is terrified, not loyal.

sentences.context: Schemes are like fruit, they require a certain ripening
sentences.simple: Tyrion's metaphor: plans are like fruit — they need time to ripen (develop) before they are ready.
sentences.grammar: Metaphor with an explanatory second clause: the comma joins the image ("fruit") to its plain meaning ("require ripening").

sentences.context: It is the sword that slays the season
sentences.simple: Septon Chayle's metaphor: the comet is like a sword that kills summer — it ends the season.
sentences.grammar: A cleft sentence ("It is … that"): the structure singles out the comet's tail as the thing doing the "slaying."

sentences.context: less you want me to see if your apple's ripe yet
sentences.simple: Yoren threatens the officer: back off, unless you want me to cut your throat — your "apple" (Adam's apple) — and see if it is "ripe" yet.
sentences.grammar: Dialect "less" for "unless," and slang where "apple" means the throat and "ripe" means ready to be cut.

sentences.context: With such do we defend the realms of men
sentences.simple: Noye is mocking the poor recruits: with men like these we are supposed to defend the kingdoms of men.
sentences.grammar: Inversion with a fronted prepositional phrase: the normal order would be "We defend the realms of men with such (men)."

sentences.context: It's her brother she'll want, as you know full well
sentences.simple: Cersei will only trade for her own brother Jaime — she wants him, not cousins. Robb knows this well.
sentences.grammar: A cleft sentence ("It's … she'll want") for emphasis, plus the tag "as you know full well" pressing a known fact.

sentences.context: the big fish eat the little fish, and I keep on paddling
sentences.simple: Varys's metaphor: the powerful destroy the weak (big fish eat little fish), but he survives by keeping on swimming.
sentences.grammar: Proverb-style parallel clauses: the sea image ("big fish eat the little fish") is paired with his own answer ("I keep on paddling").

sentences.context: Doubtless Eddard Stark thought the same
sentences.simple: Ned Stark surely thought his guards made him safe too — and he still died. They may not save Tyrion either.
sentences.grammar: Ironic one-liner: "doubtless" sounds certain, but the point is that Ned's certainty got him killed.

sentences.context: the only wolves we got to fear are the ones wear manskin
sentences.simple: Yoren's warning: the wolves we should fear are the ones wearing human skin — cruel men, like those who destroyed that village.
sentences.grammar: Dialect grammar: the missing "that/which" ("the ones [that] wear manskin") and "done" for "did" or "destroyed."

sentences.context: When a pirate grows rich enough, they make him a prince
sentences.simple: Davos's dry joke: when a pirate gets rich enough, people make him a prince instead of hanging him.
sentences.grammar: A general truth in the simple present: the "when" clause states the condition, the main clause states the ironic result.

sentences.context: For whom, she could not say
sentences.simple: Arya cried, but she could not say whose sake she was crying for — she did not know herself.
sentences.grammar: A fronted prepositional phrase ("For whom") before the verb; the normal order would be "She could not say for whom."

sentences.context: Why, sister, he never claims Jaime paid you
sentences.simple: Tyrion's private joke: Stannis never said Jaime paid you, sister — "paid" would make you a whore, and Stannis only accused you of sleeping with Jaime, not of being paid for it.
sentences.grammar: Mock-innocent correction: "Why" opens a teasing objection, and the joke turns on the word "paid," which implies prostitution.

sentences.context: Winter is coming, and you are almost a man grown
sentences.simple: The Stark words: winter is coming, and you, Bran, are almost a grown man — you have a duty.
sentences.grammar: Poetic inversion: "a man grown" flips the normal adjective order ("a grown man") for a formal, old-fashioned sound.

sentences.context: his father’s son and his brother’s heir, and almost a man grown
sentences.simple: He was the head of House Stark in Winterfell, his father's son and his brother's heir, and nearly a grown man — which is why he holds back his tears.
sentences.grammar: Old word order: 'a man grown' for 'a grown man'; the stacked phrases ('his father's son and his brother's heir') build a solemn, formal tone.

sentences.context: Dawn came cruel, a dagger of light
sentences.simple: The morning came, and it felt cruel to her — its light was like a sharp dagger stabbing into her grief.
sentences.grammar: Metaphor as action: 'cruel' and 'a dagger of light' turn the sunrise into a blade that hurts her.

sentences.context: sat a ghost in a golden crown
sentences.simple: Among them, watching and laughing with his young queen beside him, there sat a ghost wearing a golden crown — Renly, so like his dead brother Robert that Catelyn sees a ghost.
sentences.grammar: Inversion for drama: the verb 'sat' comes before its subject ('sat a ghost' instead of 'a ghost sat').

sentences.context: though not to her face, lest they be called upon to defend those words
sentences.simple: They call her 'Brienne the Beauty' — a cruel joke, since she is plain — but never to her face, because they fear she would make them fight her to prove it.
sentences.grammar: 'Lest' (for fear that) introduces a clause of feared outcome; 'they name her' is old word order for 'they call her'.

sentences.context: As if Samwell Tarly needed warning on that score
sentences.simple: As if Samwell Tarly — the most timid, gentle man in the Night's Watch — needed any warning to stay away from Craster's wives.
sentences.grammar: Ironic fragment with no main verb: 'as if' plus past tense marks something the speaker finds laughably untrue.

sentences.context: I sent the man back, but kept his tongue
sentences.simple: I sent the messenger back to Mance — but I cut out his tongue and kept it. It's nailed to that wall over there.
sentences.grammar: Deadpan literalism: 'kept his tongue' sounds like 'stayed silent' but means he cut the man's tongue out and kept it as a trophy.

sentences.context: He never gave you guest-right, so you’re not bound to him
sentences.simple: He never gave you the guest's right — food and shelter under his roof — so you are not tied to him by the sacred law of hospitality.
sentences.grammar: Compound sentence of legal logic: 'so' turns the first clause (no food or shelter given) into a conclusion about duty in the second.

sentences.context: if you sail the way you talk
sentences.simple: If you sail as badly as you boast, you will drown, and your blood will end up in the sea.
sentences.grammar: Wit in 'the way you talk': 'the way' means both his manner of speaking (boasting) and his manner of sailing — she calls him a braggart, not a sailor.

sentences.context: Only a fool humbles himself when the world is so full of men
sentences.simple: Only a fool lowers himself when the world is so full of men who are eager to do it for him.
sentences.grammar: Aphorism in the general present tense: the paradox — others are happy to humble you — delivers Theon's philosophy of pride.

sentences.context: that’s for not warning me. Next time, grow a tongue
sentences.simple: That's for not warning me. Next time, speak up and warn me — grow a tongue.
sentences.grammar: Cruel irony: Theon orders Wex to 'grow a tongue' (speak up), but Wex was born mute and cannot speak at all.

sentences.context: Brother, surely you are mistaken. Your place is at Winterfell
sentences.simple: Brother, you must be mistaken. Your place is not here among the ironborn — you were raised a Stark, and Winterfell is where you belong.
sentences.grammar: Polite words used as a weapon: 'your place' sounds kind but cuts Theon out of the ironborn — Asha is calling him a Stark-raised outsider.

sentences.context: I’m starting to believe that Robert was the clever one
sentences.simple: The gods are kind — I'm starting to believe Robert was the clever one.
sentences.grammar: Backhanded compliment: calling the famously stupid Robert 'the clever one' really means Stannis and Renly are even bigger fools for fighting each other.

sentences.context: Come join the ghosts, or be one
sentences.simple: Baker boy, here is your choice: walk into haunted Harrenhal and join the ghosts inside — or refuse, and I will kill you, and you will be a ghost yourself.
sentences.grammar: A threat dressed as a choice: 'join the ghosts' sounds like an invitation, but both options end in death — only the killer differs.

sentences.context: on an unshaven cheek. “But so do dragonslayers.”
sentences.simple: Dragons can be killed — but so can the men who try to kill them.
sentences.grammar: Ellipsis: 'so do dragonslayers' drops the verb ('dragonslayers die too'); the short reply turns Jorah's warning into a cool counter-threat.

sentences.context: Today is not the day I die
sentences.simple: There is no need to fear. I have seen the future in my green dreams, and I know I will not die today.
sentences.grammar: Calm certainty in the simple present: 'is not' states tomorrow's fact as already fixed — prophecy, not hope.

sentences.context: no one can ever claim that my sister does not love her family
sentences.simple: Well, at least no one can say my sister doesn't love her family — she loves them by sleeping with them: first her brother Jaime, and now her cousin Lancel.
sentences.grammar: Deadpan double meaning: 'loves her family' sounds innocent but means incest — the prim phrasing makes the filth funnier.

sentences.context: She had killed Chiswyck with a whisper
sentences.simple: She had killed Chiswyck with just a whisper — by naming him to Jaqen — and she would kill two more before she was done.
sentences.grammar: Past perfect ('had killed') finishes the first murder in the past, while 'would kill' looks ahead: one death done, two promised.

sentences.context: A man should never refuse to taste a peach
sentences.simple: A man should never turn down a taste of a peach — he may never get another chance. Life is short: enjoy its sweetness while you can.
sentences.grammar: A life philosophy dressed as table talk: the peach stands for pleasure, and Renly eats his last one hours before his death — dramatic irony.

sentences.context: thundered he who was notoriously without mercy
sentences.simple: 'I am not without mercy,' roared Stannis — the man who was famous for having no mercy at all.
sentences.grammar: Inversion ('thundered he' for 'he thundered') plus an instant undercut: the narrator names him 'notoriously without mercy' in the very sentence where he claims mercy.

sentences.context: Sorcery is the sauce fools spoon over failure
sentences.simple: Sorcery is just the sauce that fools spoon over their defeats to hide the taste of their own stupidity.
sentences.grammar: One long cooking metaphor: defeat is the bad meat, 'sorcery' the sauce poured over it to cover the flavor — a scornful image.

sentences.context: I thought it was Renly’s shadow at the first, but it was his brother’s
sentences.simple: I saw a shadow. At first I thought it was Renly's shadow, but it was his brother Stannis's — Stannis murdered his brother with dark magic.
sentences.grammar: The small correction ('at the first … but') is the horror: a change of owner turns a trick of the light into murder by sorcery.

sentences.context: The past. The future. The truth
sentences.simple: The past, which you cannot change. The future, which you cannot escape. The truth, which you do not want to face.
sentences.grammar: Three bare fragments with no verb at all: each noun lands like a blow — the three things dreams force you to see.

sentences.context: To go north, you must journey south
sentences.simple: To go north, you must travel south. To reach the west, you must go east. To move forward you must go back, and to touch the light you must pass beneath the shadow.
sentences.grammar: Paradox in parallel clauses: every direction is reached by its opposite — a prophecy riddle; Dany herself reads 'beneath the shadow' as Asshai.

sentences.context: King Stannis were forgotten, and King Bread ruled alone
sentences.simple: King Joffrey, King Robb, and King Stannis were forgotten — the only king the starving mob obeyed was bread.
sentences.grammar: Personification: hunger is crowned 'King Bread' — the mob's chant turns a need into the one ruler everyone follows.

sentences.context: A moon ago they were Renly’s. This morning they are yours
sentences.simple: Last year these men served Robert. A month ago they served Renly. This morning they serve you. Whose will they be tomorrow?
sentences.grammar: Shrinking time spans (last year, a moon ago, this morning) hammer the point: loyalty that changes this fast is worth nothing — Davos's question answers itself.

sentences.context: it was life I brought to Storm’s End, shaped to look like onions
sentences.simple: Last time I brought life to Storm's End, hidden to look like onions. This time I bring death, in the shape of Melisandre of Asshai.
sentences.grammar: Perfect parallel ('The last time … This time') with one word swapped — life/death: sixteen years ago Davos smuggled food through the siege; tonight he smuggles a murderer.

sentences.context: The horn that wakes the sleepers, he thought.
sentences.simple: "The horn that wakes the sleeping people," he thought. Jon hears the horn and knows the line from the Night's Watch vow.
sentences.grammar: Thought fragment: a noun phrase plus a reporting tag ("he thought"), not a complete sentence — it reports Jon's thought, not speech.

sentences.context: He lit a second candle to the Stranger, for himself.
sentences.simple: He lit another candle to the Stranger, the god of death, for himself. He fears he may die, so he prays to the death god for his own life.
sentences.grammar: Postposed purpose phrase: "for himself" is set apart at the end, so the shock lands last — the candle to the death god is for his own death.

sentences.context: Rooth Bolton thought to croth the river
sentences.simple: Read it as: "Captives. Roose Bolton planned to cross the river, but my Brave Companions cut his front line to pieces." Vargo Hoat has a lisp: his "s" sounds come out as "th."
sentences.grammar: Eye dialect: the spelling copies a lisp ("s" written as "th"), so "Captiths" means captives and "Rooth" means Roose.

sentences.context: A goat has no loyalty.
sentences.simple: "A goat" means Vargo Hoat, whose sellsword badge is a goat. Jaqen is saying Hoat cannot be trusted to stay loyal.
sentences.grammar: Metonymy: "a goat" stands for a person (Vargo Hoat), named by the animal on his badge.

sentences.context: his is the song of ice and fire.
sentences.simple: He is the promised prince from the old prophecy, and his story is the song of ice and fire.
sentences.grammar: Parallel prophecy lines: two balanced statements joined by "and," spoken in the flat tone of a vision.

sentences.context: three heads has the dragon
sentences.simple: The dragon has three heads. (Normal word order would be: "the dragon has three heads.")
sentences.grammar: Inversion for mystery: the object ("three heads") is pulled to the front, echoing the three-headed dragon on the Targaryen flag.

sentences.context: it might be you’ll need them swords again
sentences.simple: "Burn the bodies," the girl said again, stubbornly. "If you do not, they may rise again as wights, and you will need those swords again."
sentences.grammar: Dialect grammar: "them swords" means "those swords," and "it might be you'll" means "you might" — a conditional without "if."

sentences.context: the gods hate kinslayers, even when they kill unknowing.
sentences.simple: The gods hate people who kill their own family, even when they do it without knowing.
sentences.grammar: Bare proverb style: a short general truth with no introduction; "unknowing" is an adjective used where an adverb ("unknowingly") would stand.

sentences.context: The blood is the seal of your womanhood.
sentences.simple: The blood is the proof that you are now a woman.
sentences.grammar: Metaphor as definition: "is" joins two nouns ("blood" = "seal"), saying one thing stands as the sign of another.

sentences.context: Love is poison. A sweet poison, yes, but it will kill you
sentences.simple: Love is like poison. It tastes sweet, yes, but it will kill you just the same. Cersei means love makes you weak and gets you killed.
sentences.grammar: Hammer-blow short sentences plus a fragment ("A sweet poison, yes") for a cold, final warning.

sentences.context: Not always, came the silent shout. Not before the crow.
sentences.simple: "Not always," said the quiet voice that made no sound. "Not before the crow." The tree's face did not always have three eyes — not before the crow came to it.
sentences.grammar: Inverted reporting ("came the silent shout" flips verb before subject); the answer is two broken fragments, not full sentences.

sentences.context: “Is your red flower still blooming?”
sentences.simple: "Is your red flower still blooming?" Cersei is really asking whether Sansa is still having her monthly period — she uses a garden image to hide the blunt question.
sentences.grammar: Euphemistic question: a flower image ("red flower blooming") hides a blunt question about menstruation.

sentences.context: Had he been admiral, he might have done it all differently.
sentences.simple: If he had been the admiral, he might have fought the battle in a different way. Davos imagines how he would have done it.
sentences.grammar: Inversion for a past unreal condition: "Had he been" means "If he had been" — the "if" is dropped and the verb moves first.

sentences.context: pots of burning pitch, arcing out over the river trailing threads of flame
sentences.simple: A group of flickering orange "birds" flew up from the castle, twenty or thirty of them. They were not birds at all — they were pots of burning tar, flying over the river with lines of flame trailing behind them.
sentences.grammar: Delayed identification: the sentence first shows "birds," then an appositive ("pots of burning pitch") reveals what they really are.

sentences.context: The Warrior must have been listening.
sentences.simple: The Warrior, the god of battle, must have heard our prayer. Davos means their ramming attack worked because the god helped.
sentences.grammar: Modal perfect of belief: "must have been" shows Davos is sure the god answered, not that he saw it happen.

sentences.context: turned proud ships into funeral pyres and men into living torches
sentences.simple: The touch of wildfire turned fine ships into burning piles for the dead, and living men into burning torches.
sentences.grammar: Metaphor chain with parallel "into" phrases: "kiss," "funeral pyres," and "living torches" pile three fire images onto one burning.

sentences.context: Eyes of wildfire, Sansa thought.
sentences.simple: "Eyes of wildfire," Sansa thought. Cersei has been drinking heavily; her eyes are bright and feverish, and to Sansa they look like the green wildfire flames burning on the river.
sentences.grammar: Thought fragment: a noun phrase with a reporting tag ("Sansa thought"), not a complete sentence.

sentences.context: three treasons… once for blood and once for gold and once for love
sentences.simple: The warlocks spoke softly of three betrayals: one for family (blood), one for money (gold), and one for love. Dany will be betrayed three times.
sentences.grammar: Ellipsis with anaphora: "…" skips the details, then "once for…" repeats the same shape three times like a prophecy.

sentences.context: little as he may like it
sentences.simple: Robb will hate doing it, but he must do it anyway: make peace with the Lannisters, give up his crown, and kneel to the king.
sentences.grammar: Concessive compression: "little as he may like it" means "however little he likes it" — a shortened "however + adjective" clause tucked at the sentence end.

sentences.context: Must I have your tongue out?
sentences.simple: Bolton is threatening to cut out her tongue. He really means: "Must I have your tongue cut out?"
sentences.grammar: Ellipsis in a threat: the verb "cut" is left out ("your tongue [cut] out"), and a question is used to give an order.

sentences.context: His throat, it must be his throat, but he’s too tall
sentences.simple: Arya is thinking fast as she plans the killing: his throat — it must be his throat — but he's too tall; she'll never reach it.
sentences.grammar: Fragmented inner monologue: broken, self-correcting phrases ("his throat, it must be his throat") that copy the rhythm of racing thought.

sentences.context: and to him shall go all the lands, rights, and incomes
sentences.simple: And all the lands, rights, and incomes of House Caron shall go to him.
sentences.grammar: Formal inversion: "to him shall go" flips the normal order ("shall go to him") to sound grand, as in official decrees.

sentences.context: which made the alchemist no more a true lord than Varys was
sentences.simple: ...which meant the alchemist was exactly as much a true lord as Varys was — that is, not a true lord at all.
sentences.grammar: Negative comparison: "no more X than Y" sets X and Y equal at zero — as much a true lord as Varys, which is not one at all.

sentences.context: Unless they are made to. Unless my brother and my uncle
sentences.simple: Unless they are forced to accept him — the river lords would never follow Littlefinger willingly.
sentences.grammar: Ellipsis: the verb phrase is cut off ("unless they are made to [obey him]"), leaving "by force" for the reader to fill in.

sentences.context: She’ll give you all a warm welcome, I have no doubt
sentences.simple: Theon is being sarcastic: Asha despises him and his men are deserting to her — there will be no warm welcome at all.
sentences.grammar: Sarcasm: saying the opposite of the truth — "warm welcome" means its cold opposite, since Asha will show them none.

sentences.context: Would that I had thrust a sword through your belly
sentences.simple: I wish I had killed you with a sword instead of training you to use one.
sentences.grammar: Old-style wish ("would that I had…"): an optative subjunctive expressing regret — "I wish I had done this instead."

sentences.context: The noose I wore was not made of hempen rope
sentences.simple: Theon is speaking in metaphor: his "noose" was his childhood as a Stark hostage — no rope around his neck, but he felt trapped and chafed raw just the same.
sentences.grammar: Extended metaphor: a real noose is a hangman's rope; here it stands for Theon's trapped childhood as a hostage.

sentences.context: Would a foe bring such fine gifts?
sentences.simple: Red Helm is being sarcastic: his "fine gifts" are three corpses — the bodies of Ser Rodrik, Leobald Tallhart, and Cley Cerwyn.
sentences.grammar: Sarcastic rhetorical question: asks "would an enemy bring gifts?" while displaying dead bodies as the "gifts."

sentences.context: When the old fool gave me his hand, I took half his arm instead
sentences.simple: "Gave me his hand" means shook hands in truce; "took half his arm" means Ramsay cut Ser Rodrik's arm off at the elbow.
sentences.grammar: Grim wordplay (pun): the handshake ("gave me his hand") is twisted into amputation ("took half his arm").

sentences.context: They do not neither. They beat them, I bet,
sentences.simple: They don't. (Tysha's lowborn speech uses two negatives; they strengthen the "no" instead of canceling it.)
sentences.grammar: Double negative in lowborn speech: "do not neither" means simply "don't" — the two negatives strengthen, not cancel, the refusal.

sentences.context: felt strong enough to face his face
sentences.simple: He felt brave enough to confront (face) his ruined appearance (his face).
sentences.grammar: Pun on "face": to "face" (bravely confront) his "face" (his wounded countenance).

sentences.context: but if the Wall should ever fall, all the fires will go out
sentences.simple: Qhorin means the Wall keeps everyone safe: their little campfire will die soon, but if the Wall itself falls, every fire in the world — every warm, safe home — goes out with it.
sentences.grammar: Parallel contrast: the small campfire that "will soon go out" stands beside the great "fires" of all homes — the Wall guards them all.

sentences.context: When I see him next. I swear it
sentences.simple: Qhorin knows he will not see Mormont again — he expects to die here. The promise is a kind lie to comfort Jon.
sentences.grammar: A gentle lie: Qhorin promises to speak to Mormont while knowing he will die here — the future tense hides certain death.

sentences.context: “… sharp,” he said, lifting his maimed fingers.
sentences.simple: With his dying breath Qhorin answers his own twice-asked question, "Is your sword sharp, Jon Snow?" — yes, it was sharp enough.
sentences.grammar: Dying ellipsis: the single word "… sharp" completes Qhorin's own twice-asked question, "Is your sword sharp?"

sentences.context: This scrawny skin of mine’s the only one I got
sentences.simple: This thin body is the only one I have, so I won't risk it.
sentences.grammar: Rough dialect: "mine's" is "of mine is" and "I got" is "I've got" (I have) — ungrammatical forms marking Osha's lowborn speech.

sentences.context: a sellsword, black of hair and heart,
sentences.simple: Black-haired, and black-hearted — cruel and without pity. The appendix sums Bronn up in five words.
sentences.grammar: Parallel pairing ("black of hair and heart"): one word of body, one of soul — black-haired and black-hearted (cruel).
